figures.title: AlexNet Architecture
figures.caption: **AlexNet Architecture**: Two parallel GPU streams process $224{\times}224$ input images through convolutional layers (green blocks) that extract spatial features at decreasing resolutions, converging through three fully connected layers to 1,000 output classes. Because each stream holds half of the network, the figure also shows how the model was partitioned across two GPUs. Adapted from @krizhevsky2012imagenet.
figures.alt: 3D diagram of AlexNet with two parallel GPU streams. Green blocks show convolutional layers decreasing from 224x224 input. Red kernels overlay green blocks. Right side shows three dense layers converging to 1000 outputs.

figures.title: Algorithmic Efficiency Trajectory
figures.caption: **Algorithmic Efficiency Trajectory**: Each point shows how much less training compute an ImageNet architecture needed than AlexNet to reach AlexNet-level accuracy, so height measures algorithmic progress with hardware speed held out. Most later architectures sit well above AlexNet, although individual points vary; VGG-11 needed more compute than AlexNet. The dashed line is a least-squares exponential fit to the measured points. figures.title: The Era of Scale
figures.caption: **The Era of Scale**: Each point plots a third-party training-compute estimate (FLOPs) for a notable model against its publication year on a log scale. Runs below $10^{22}$ FLOPs appear in blue; larger runs appear in red. The dashed line is a least-squares fit to these points and doubles every `{python} TrainingComputeGrowthFigure.doubling_months_str` months. From AlexNet (2012) to GPT-4-class training scale (2023), compute requirements increased by roughly `{python} TrainingComputeGrowthFigure.compute_growth_order_str` orders of magnitude (about `{python} TrainingComputeGrowthFigure.compute_growth_m_str` times). This endpoint comparison is distinct from training-compute trend studies [@amodei2018aicompute; @sevilla2022] and is used here to motivate the specialized infrastructure described in this book. Data from Epoch AI's Notable AI Models database [@epochai2026notable].
figures.alt: Scatter plot of training-compute estimates on a logarithmic scale from 2012 to 2025. Blue points mark runs below 10 to the 22 FLOPs; red points mark larger runs. A dashed least-squares fit line rises through the points.

figures.title: Fifty Years of Microprocessor Trends
figures.caption: **Fifty Years of Microprocessor Trends**: Transistor count, single-thread performance (SPECint benchmark score), clock frequency, typical power, and logical core count of microprocessors from 1971 to 2021 on a logarithmic axis. Transistor counts keep rising after the mid-2000s while frequency and typical power level off and single-thread performance slows; the gray band marks the end of Dennard scaling, after which added transistors went into more cores. Data from @rupp2022microprocessor.
figures.alt: Scatter plot on a logarithmic vertical axis from 1970 to 2022 with five series: transistors in thousands rising steadily to about 10 to the 7.7, single-thread performance rising and then flattening after about 2005, frequency in megahertz flattening near 3,000 to 5,000 after 2005, typical power in watts leveling near 100, and logical cores staying at 1 until about 2005 and then rising. A gray vertical band near 2005 is labeled end of Dennard scaling.

figures.title: Smart Doorbell Constraint Scorecard
figures.caption: **Smart Doorbell Constraint Scorecard**: Each bar is demand over supply, so the dashed line marks the point where a level is exactly saturated. The model occupies a small fraction of the ESP32-S3's 4 MB flash budget (Level 1: PASS), but its 101 ms latency (25 MFLOP of compute plus fixed overhead) is twice a tightened 50 ms budget for a responsive chime (Level 2: FAIL), even though it clears the scenario's canonical 200 ms budget.
figures.alt: Horizontal bar chart of demand over supply with a dashed saturation line at 1.0. The latency (SLA) bar is red and extends to about twice the line. The memory (flash) bar is green and short, far below the line.

figures.title: Energy per Inference Across Deployment Tiers
figures.caption: **Energy per Inference Across Deployment Tiers**: An eight-order-of-magnitude energy gap separates always-on TinyML keyword spotting (~10 µJ) from a cloud foundation-model query (~1 kJ) on a log scale. The three vision bars are device-level estimates (the device's power draw at its modeled utilization over the batch-1 inference window, counting the whole phone, the edge tier's NVIDIA Jetson embedded GPU module, or the A100 card) from the same analytical model used throughout this chapter; the two endpoints are scenario anchors. The tasks and accounting boundaries differ, so these bars illustrate energy scales rather than a controlled hardware-efficiency or offload comparison.
figures.alt: Horizontal log-scale bar chart of energy per inference for five workloads across four deployment paradigms. TinyML keyword spotting is about 10 microjoules; Mobile MobileNetV2 and Edge ResNet-50 fall in the single and low tens of millijoules; Cloud ResNet-50 on an A100 is under a tenth of a joule; and a cloud LLM query anchor is about 1 kilojoule, eight orders of magnitude above keyword spotting.

figures.title: From Neuron to Machine
figures.caption: **From Neuron to Machine**: One neuron is a dot product between an input row and a weight column. A layer applied to a batch stacks those dot products into one matrix multiply whose cost is the product of batch size, input width, and output width. On an accelerator, a tile of the weight matrix stays inside an array of multiply-accumulate units while input rows stream through, so the batch, not the neuron, sets how much arithmetic each fetched weight pays for.
figures.alt: Three panels left to right. One neuron: a horizontal input bar of size 1 by n-in times a vertical weight bar of size n-in by 1, labeled a dot product of n-in MACs. One layer, one batch: matrix X of size B by n-in times W of size n-in by n-out equals Z of size B by n-out, labeled B times n-in times n-out MACs. On the machine: four input rows stream into a four-by-four grid of green multiply-accumulate cells holding a weight tile, producing Z on the right; caption says each weight is fetched once and reused by all B rows.
figures.systems_goal: Show how batching amortizes weight-tile fetches over multiple input rows.

figures.title: Recurrent Neural Network Unfolding

figures.title: Transformer Architecture (Encoder-Decoder)
figures.caption: **Transformer Architecture (Encoder-Decoder)**: The encoder (left, repeated $\LayerCount$ times) consists of multi-head attention followed by feed-forward layers, each with residual connections (arrows bypassing blocks) and layer normalization. figures.title: Prefill and Decode
figures.caption: **Prefill and Decode**: Prefill (left) runs the whole prompt through the model in one pass of matrix-matrix products, reusing every weight across all prompt tokens, and writes each prompt token's keys and values to the KV cache. Decode (right) then generates one token per step: each output becomes the next input, each step runs matrix-vector products that re-read every weight, and each step reads the whole cache and appends one entry. The first phase is usually compute-bound; the second is usually bandwidth-bound at small batch.

Captions beneath read: weights reused across every prompt token, usually compute-bound; and every weight and the whole cache re-read for each new token, usually bandwidth-bound at small batch.

figures.title: Data Movement Primitives
figures.caption: **Data Movement Primitives**: Four fundamental patterns govern information flow in neural network computation. Broadcast (top-left) replicates a single value to all destinations, used when sharing weights across batch elements. Scatter (top-right) distributes distinct elements to different destinations, enabling work partitioning. Gather (bottom-left) collects distributed values to a single location, as in attention pooling. Reduction (bottom-right) combines multiple values through aggregation (sum, max), appearing in gradient synchronization and attention scoring. Because moving data costs more than computing on it, these patterns are primary optimization targets.
figures.alt: Four diagrams with nodes and arrows. Broadcast: one red square to four nodes. Scatter: four colored squares to four nodes. Gather: four nodes with colored squares to one. Reduction: four nodes labeled 1, 3, 5, and 7 combine into one node labeled 16.
figures.systems_goal: Distinguish replication, partitioning, collection, and arithmetic aggregation in data movement.

figures.title: Tensor Memory Layout
figures.caption: **Tensor Memory Layout**: A $2{\times}3$ tensor can be stored in linear memory using either row-major (C-style) or column-major (Fortran-style) ordering. Strides count elements skipped in each dimension, so i $\times$ stride[0] + j $\times$ stride[1] gives an element offset. Multiplying by the element size gives the byte offset from the storage origin. The choice of layout affects which traversals access neighboring elements efficiently.

figures.title: Floating-Point Bit Layouts
figures.caption: **Floating-Point Bit Layouts**: Bit allocation trades dynamic range against significand precision. FP32 uses 8 exponent and 23 fraction bits. figures.title: Hardware Specialization Timeline
figures.caption: **Hardware Specialization Timeline**: Computing architectures evolve through recurring cycles of specialization and integration across five eras. Many of these capabilities later appear alongside CPUs in broader systems, even when the specialized units remain distinct.

figures.title: The Rising Ridge

As compute capability grows faster than memory bandwidth, the ridge point rises from V100 through H100 and remains high on B200. This trend explains why architectures with high data reuse flourish while low-reuse workloads face a growing performance penalty.

figures.title: The Business Cost Curve
figures.caption: **The Business Cost Curve**: An equal-class-weighted illustrative cost index vs. classification threshold. Technical metrics like ROC curves hide the economic reality: errors have different costs. Here, a false negative (missed fraud) costs \$500, while a false positive (blocked user) costs \$100. The system flags a transaction as fraud when its score exceeds the threshold, so a lower threshold flags more transactions. Because missing fraud is $5\times$ more costly, the optimal threshold shifts left of center, making the system more aggressive at flagging suspicious transactions and accepting more false positives to minimize expensive misses. With equal costs the optimum would sit at threshold = 0.50; the asymmetry pulls it toward threshold $\approx 0.34$. A population expected cost would also weight each term by class prevalence. MLOps tunes thresholds as costs and prevalence change.
figures.alt: Line chart showing an equal-class-weighted illustrative cost index vs. classification threshold from 0 to 1. Three curves are plotted: false positive cost index (dashed blue) decreasing sigmoidally from left to right, false negative cost index (dashed red) increasing sigmoidally from left to right, and total cost index (solid violet) as their sum forming a U-shape. The optimal threshold is marked with a green dot left of center where the total index is minimized.

figures.title: The scale discontinuity
figures.caption: **The scale discontinuity**: On a single machine (left), the usual binding constraint is the memory wall between the accelerators and their high-bandwidth memory, and there are no peers to wait for. In a fleet (right), nodes exchange state over a shared network fabric under a scheduler that places the job and recovers it, so the three C$^3$ roles appear as separate components. The fabric can become the binding network wall, and failed and slow nodes become routine events that hold back the whole job.

figures.title: Retryable tasks vs. shared training steps
figures.caption: **Retryable tasks vs. shared training steps**: Map tasks (left) deliver their outputs independently, so a failed task is re-run on its own while the others finish; its missing output delays only the reducers that need it. In synchronous data-parallel training (right), the AllReduce needs every worker's gradient before the shared update can proceed, so a slow worker on the critical path holds the whole step and the healthy workers wait. How much the step stretches depends on overlap and the other costs of the step.
figures.alt: Two timelines with time running left to right. Left, MapReduce: map tasks 1 and 2 run, emit a green output square, and are labeled done; map task 3 runs briefly, is marked failed with a red cross, and then a re-run alone bar on the same lane emits its output, which feeds a reduce bar on the lane below. Right, synchronous training: workers 0 and 1 finish their compute bars early and then show gray wait segments, while worker 2 runs a long red dashed bar labeled slow; all three bars end at an amber AllReduce band, after which an update bar runs on the lane below.

figures.title: Model training compute trends
figures.caption: **Model training compute trends**: Training compute has grown exponentially, accelerating dramatically in the deep learning era. The fitted trends shift from roughly 1.4$\times$ per year before 2010, close to Moore's Law (a doubling about every 2 years), to roughly 4$\times$ per year inside the deep learning era, far steeper than Moore's Law. The fastest stretch was steeper still. Within the 2012--2019 frontier subset measured by an earlier study [@amodei2018ai], compute doubled approximately every 3.4 months. This trajectory explains why efficiency has become a strategic imperative rather than an optional optimization.
figures.alt: Scatter plot of training compute from 1950 to 2025 on log scale. figures.title: Tensor Core tiling strategy
figures.caption: **Tensor Core tiling strategy**: Read left to right. To compute one tile of the output matrix $\GemmOutputMatrix$, the kernel streams matching slices of $\GemmLeftOperand$ and $\GemmRightOperand$ from HBM (left) into the SM's shared memory (center), where Tensor Core instructions (right) multiply them many times over while the FP32 partial sums for that $\GemmOutputMatrix$ tile stay in registers. Only after every slice along the shared $\GemmInnerDimension$ dimension has been accumulated is the finished $\GemmOutputMatrix$ tile written back to HBM once, so each byte fetched from HBM feeds many multiply-accumulate operations. The tile shapes shown ($128 \times 32$ slices, a $128 \times 128$ output tile) are one typical choice; kernels tune them to the chip.
figures.alt: Three panels joined by arrows. Left, HBM with full matrices at 3.35 TB/s: matrix A with a row band split into K slices, matrix B with a column band split into K slices, one slice of each dark, and matrix C with one outlined output tile. Center, shared memory with 228 KB per SM: a tall A tile of 128 by 32 and a wide B tile of 32 by 128. Right, Tensor Cores and registers: a grid of small MMA instruction squares above a C tile of 128 by 128 holding FP32 sums. A dashed loop above the panels returns from the Tensor Cores to HBM, labeled repeat per K slice: load the next pair. A solid arrow below returns from the Tensor Cores to C in HBM, labeled after the last slice: write the C tile once.

figures.title: HBM 3D-stacked architecture
figures.caption: **HBM 3D-stacked architecture**: Left: high-bandwidth memory stacks DRAM dies on a base logic die, links them vertically with through-silicon vias (TSVs), and places the stack on a silicon interposer beside the GPU die, so each stack reaches the GPU over a 1,024-bit interface only millimeters long. Right: DDR5 instead sits on a DIMM across the motherboard, reached over a 64-bit channel through centimeters of board trace. The wider, shorter path raises bandwidth and lowers energy per bit, but HBM bandwidth and capacity remain finite, so the memory wall moves rather than disappears.

Right, DDR5 across the board: a CPU with its memory controller and a DIMM holding several DRAM chips stand on a motherboard, joined by a thin trace through the board labeled 64 bits wide, centimeters long.

figures.title: Intra-node GPU topology comparison
figures.caption: **Intra-node GPU topology comparison**: Three ways to wire eight GPUs inside one node. Left: a ring gives each GPU only two links, so traffic between distant GPUs passes through up to four hops. Center: a full mesh reaches every peer in one hop but needs $\AcceleratorsPerNode-1$ links per GPU and $\AcceleratorsPerNode(\AcceleratorsPerNode-1)/2$ links in total, which becomes impractical to route beyond about eight GPUs. figures.title: The infrastructure bandwidth hierarchy
figures.caption: **The infrastructure bandwidth hierarchy**: Concentric zones place each tier an ML workload crosses farther from the accelerator's own memory. figures.title: The power delivery path
figures.caption: **The power delivery path**: Energy passes through five conversion stages between the medium-voltage grid and the sub-volt supply at the GPU die, and each stage loses a few percent as heat; the band's height is drawn proportional to the power it carries. The per-stage losses shown are illustrative round values, not measurements of a particular facility; compounded, they lose about a fifth of the power, so delivering 1 MW to the dies draws about 1.3 MW before cooling. PUE uses an IT-equipment boundary and includes facility conversion losses as well as cooling; these losses must not be counted twice. The critical engineering challenge is the rack power distribution unit (PDU) to voltage regulator module (VRM) transition, where 10--40 kW of power must be delivered within a single cabinet.
figures.alt: A horizontal band of power flows left to right through five narrow conversion stages: from the utility grid at 13 kV and up, through a transformer to 480 V AC, a UPS at 480 V backup, a rack PDU to 240 V AC, a server PSU to 12 V DC, and a VRM to under 1 V, ending at a dark block labeled GPU dies. The band starts about 1.3 MW tall and ends at 1 MW, and at each stage a thin orange strip peels off downward as heat, labeled about 5, 3, 3, 5, and 8 percent. A dark bracket and a pale tinted region mark the span from the rack PDU through the VRM, labeled inside each cabinet, 10 to 40 kW per rack.

figures.title: Pod-scale network topologies
figures.caption: **Pod-scale network topologies**: Two dominant ways to wire a pod. Left: a switched fat-tree, drawn here as a two-tier leaf and spine fabric in which every leaf switch connects to every spine switch and has as many uplinks as node ports, so any half of the nodes can talk to the other half at full rate (full bisection bandwidth). InfiniBand clusters such as DGX SuperPOD use this design, and larger pods add a third, core tier above the spines. Right: a 2D torus wires each node directly to its four neighbors, and the dashed stubs wrap each row and column around to its opposite edge; bisection bandwidth grows only as $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\ClusterNodeCount})$, so the torus is cheaper at scale but rewards workloads with strong locality, as in Google TPU pods. The choice shapes which parallelism strategies run efficiently.
figures.alt: Two panels. Left, Switched fat-tree: four spine switches in a top row, four leaf switches below with a link from every leaf to every spine, and four nodes under each leaf; leaf L1's four uplinks and four node links are highlighted, and the footer reads L1: 4 uplinks = 4 node ports, full bisection bandwidth. Right, 2D torus: a four-by-four grid of nodes joined to their horizontal and vertical neighbors, with dashed stubs at every row and column end marking wrap-around links; a dashed vertical bisection cut runs down the middle, and the four row links it crosses plus the row wrap-around stubs are highlighted. The footer reads bisection grows as the square root of the node count, each node links to 4 neighbors.

figures.title: The five-level network model for ML training
figures.caption: **The five-level network model for ML training**: Read from the bottom up, each level builds on the one below and becomes more abstract. Level 1 moves bits over wires and optics; Level 2 turns links into reliable, low-overhead transfers between accelerators; Level 3 arranges switches into a topology; Level 4 governs how the fabric behaves under load and congestion; and Level 5 integrates all of them into a production cluster.
figures.alt: Five stacked horizontal bands, labeled L1 at the bottom to L5 at the top, with an upward arrow labeled more abstract. L1, wire and link: PAM4 SerDes, copper DAC, AOC, optics. L2, transport: RDMA, RoCEv2, GPUDirect, alpha-beta cost model. L3, switch and topology: fat-tree, rail-optimized, Dragonfly, torus. L4, fabric behavior: PFC, ECN and DCQCN, incast, adaptive routing. L5, cluster design: pod integration, job placement, failure domains. Beside each band a small schematic shows the level's concrete form: L1, a four-level stepped waveform between two transceivers labeled SerDes; L2, a GPU and its NIC, both labeled, sending to a remote NIC and GPU; L3, two switches linked to all four switches below them; L4, three converging inputs feeding a nearly full queue, with a dashed red arrow labeled PAUSE leaving the queue and pointing back over the inputs; L5, a row of six racks joined by a common bar.

figures.title: From NRZ to PAM4 signaling
figures.caption: **From NRZ to PAM4 signaling**: Both panels send six symbols in the same time over the same total voltage swing. NRZ (left) uses two levels and carries one bit per symbol, 6 bits in all; PAM4 (right) uses four levels and carries two bits per symbol, 12 bits in all, doubling the data rate without raising the symbol rate. The cost is noise margin: adjacent PAM4 levels sit one third as far apart (arrows), so high-speed links need forward error correction (FEC), which adds to the fabric's fixed $\MessageStartupLatency$ latency.
figures.alt: Two waveform panels with six equal symbol slots marked by dashed vertical lines. Left, NRZ: a square wave switching between levels 1 and 0, with one tall shaded band between the two levels and an arrow labeled full swing; below, a strip of six cells holds the bits 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, labeled 6 bits. Right, PAM4: a stepped wave among four levels labeled 00, 01, 10, and 11, with three thin shaded bands between adjacent levels and an arrow labeled one-third swing across one band; below, a strip of twelve cells grouped in pairs holds two bits per symbol, labeled 12 bits.

figures.title: Traditional TCP/IP vs. RDMA verbs stacks
figures.caption: **Traditional TCP/IP vs. RDMA verbs stacks**: Read each stack top to bottom through the user-space, kernel, and hardware bands. In the illustrated copied TCP/IP socket path (left), a send enters the kernel through a system call, the payload is copied into kernel socket buffers and again toward the NIC's transmit ring, and the CPU runs the transport protocol in software. figures.title: A PFC deadlock from a cyclic buffer dependency
figures.caption: **A PFC deadlock from a cyclic buffer dependency**: Four switch queues form the cycle of @eq-network-buffer-dependency-cycle. figures.title: Parallel file system architecture
figures.caption: **Parallel file system architecture**: A client makes one metadata request (MDS $\to$ MDT) to learn a file's stripe map, then reads the stripes directly from the object storage servers (OSS $\to$ OST) in parallel. Each OST holds every Nth stripe of the file in round-robin order, so consecutive stripes (dark) sit on different servers and one client reads them at once. The shared data path lets every client draw on every OSS, so aggregate bandwidth grows with the number of servers while metadata traffic stays on a separate path.
figures.alt: Architecture diagram with compute clients on the left, a metadata server and a column of object storage servers in the middle, and storage targets on the right. A violet line labeled lookup runs from client 1 to the metadata server, whose target holds a stripe map listing OSTs 1 through N. Green lines join every client through a shared vertical bus to every object storage server. Each object storage target holds stripe tiles of one file: OST 1 holds 0, N, 2N; OST 2 holds 1, N+1, 2N+1; and so on to OST N, with the first tile of each target filled dark green.

figures.title: Four central collective primitives
figures.caption: **Four central collective primitives**: Standardized patterns for group communication in distributed systems. In each panel the four rows are ranks 0 to 3, read left to right from each rank's input, through the collective, to what each rank holds afterward. (1) AllReduce: all aggregate and all receive the result. (2) AllGather: all send to all and concatenate. (3) ReduceScatter: all aggregate and results are distributed in shards. (4) AllToAll: every process sends unique data to every other process. The two foundational primitives Broadcast (rank 0 sends to all) and Reduce (all aggregate to rank 0) compose the patterns shown here and are defined in the surrounding prose.
figures.alt: Four panels, AllReduce, AllGather, ReduceScatter, and AllToAll, each with rows for ranks 0 to 3. Each row shows the rank's input buffer as small tiles, an amber collective band, and the output buffer. AllReduce: four chunks a to d per rank become four green sums on every rank. AllGather: one chunk per rank becomes four chunks a to d on every rank. ReduceScatter: four chunks per rank become one green sum per rank, sum a on rank 0 through sum d on rank 3. AllToAll: rank i's chunks a_i to d_i are transposed so rank 0 holds a0 to a3, rank 1 holds b0 to b3, and so on. Chunk a has a bold outline in every panel.

figures.title: Hierarchical AllReduce
figures.caption: **Hierarchical AllReduce**: Three-phase decomposition that exploits the intra-node/inter-node bandwidth gap. Phase 1 performs intra-node aggregation over NVLink (an NVLink ring acting as a ReduceScatter that leaves each GPU holding a node-shard partial sum), leaving a payload of $\CollectivePayloadSize/\AcceleratorsPerNode$ on each of the $\AcceleratorsPerNode$ GPUs per node. Phase 2 runs an AllReduce across corresponding GPUs using InfiniBand. Phase 3 completes intra-node distribution over NVLink (the AllGather that returns each GPU to the full result). The schematic shows two representative ranks per node; the same decomposition applies to $\AcceleratorsPerNode$ ranks.
figures.alt: Three panels for the three phases, each showing Node 0 above Node 1, each node holding GPU 0 and GPU 1 cards with two shard tiles. Thick NVLink bars join the GPUs inside a node and dashed InfiniBand links join corresponding GPUs across nodes; in each panel only the links in use are amber and the others are light gray. Phase 1, ReduceScatter: NVLink lit, each GPU holds one half-filled node partial sum. Phase 2, Shard AllReduce: InfiniBand lit, one half-filled shard tile rides each inter-node link, and each GPU ends with one green full sum. Phase 3, AllGather: NVLink lit, every GPU holds both green full sums.

figures.title: Dimension-ordered reduction on a torus topology
figures.caption: **Dimension-ordered reduction on a torus topology**: In a 2D torus mesh ($4 \times 4$ node grid representing a simplified TPU pod slice), AllReduce proceeds sequentially along orthogonal dimensions. Phase 1 (orange) executes four parallel horizontal rings across the X dimension ($2(\TorusFirstAxisChipCount-1) = 6$ steps). Phase 2 (slate) then executes four parallel vertical rings across the Y dimension ($2(\TorusSecondAxisChipCount-1) = 6$ steps) on the row-aggregated partial sums. Dashed stubs mark the torus wrap-around links, each leaving one edge of the grid and re-entering at the opposite edge. This dimension-ordered decomposition needs 12 startup rounds against 30 for a 16-rank 1D global ring, a $2.5\times$ reduction, but each axis processes the full message, so its bandwidth time is $3\CollectivePayloadSize/\LinkBandwidth$ for this grid.

figures.title: Endpoint and in-network reduction
figures.caption: **Endpoint and in-network reduction**: The upstream half of a reduction over four GPUs. (a) Switches only forward packets, so every full gradient tensor crosses the upper links and converges on one reducer GPU, which does all the arithmetic. figures.title: Communication-computation overlap
figures.caption: **Communication-computation overlap**: The backward pass runs from the last layer to the first, and each layer's gradient AllReduce launches as soon as that layer finishes, so it runs on the network while the GPU computes the next layer's gradients. The first layer finishes last and has no computation left to hide behind, so its AllReduce is exposed before the optimizer step. Overlap succeeds only when the nonoverlappable overhead ($\SymmetricMessageOverhead$) is small, leaving the bulk transfer free to proceed concurrently. Durations are schematic.

A bracket marks the first three AllReduces as hidden behind backward compute, and a shaded band labeled exposed covers the last o slice and AllReduce L1. A key notes that o is nonoverlappable overhead that occupies the GPU.

figures.title: The memory wall

figures.title: The 3D parallelism cube
figures.caption: **The 3D parallelism cube**: The configuration space decomposes cluster training across three orthogonal axes: tensor parallelism ($\TensorParallelDegree$, intra-layer sharding), pipeline parallelism ($\PipelineParallelDegree$, sequential stage partitioning), and data parallelism ($\DataParallelDegree$, batch replication). figures.title: Data parallelism implementation pipeline
figures.caption: **Data parallelism implementation pipeline**: The five-stage workflow for data-parallel training: (1) partition the global batch, (2) assign sharded mini-batches to individual GPUs, (3) compute independent forward and backward passes to produce local gradients $\MinibatchGradient_i$, (4) execute an AllReduce collective across the cluster to obtain the average gradient $\GlobalBatchGradient$, and (5) update parameters identically across all devices. This strategy preserves the mathematical semantics of single-device SGD while distributing the compute burden.

A green global batch of B equals 128, drawn as sixteen sample tiles in four groups, sends one group of 32 samples to each GPU. Each GPU card holds an identical four-layer model replica and runs forward and backward passes, producing a small signed bar vector g0 to g3 whose bars differ from lane to lane. All four vectors enter one tall amber AllReduce block labeled g global equals one over N times the sum of g i, ring. Every lane then shows the same averaged bar vector g global feeding an update theta card, with the note identical theta on every GPU.

figures.title: Distributed synchronization models
figures.caption: **Distributed synchronization models**: The timelines compare three synchronization strategies. Top: bulk synchronous parallel (BSP) forces all workers to wait at a global barrier every step. Middle: stale synchronous parallel (SSP) allows workers to proceed up to $\StalenessBound$ steps ahead of the slowest worker. Bottom: asynchronous parallel (ASP) execution removes the global update barrier while allowing gradient staleness; communication and resource contention can still delay progress.
figures.alt: Timeline diagram with three panels of four worker rows, in which worker W3 takes longer per iteration than the others. Top, BSP: after every iteration the faster workers sit in red-hatched wait blocks until W3, labeled slow in red, reaches a global barrier. Middle, SSP with s equal to 1: the faster workers run freely until they would lead W3 by more than one iteration, then pause briefly. Bottom, ASP: every worker runs without waiting, so the faster workers finish eight iterations while W3 finishes six.

figures.title: ZeRO memory reduction
figures.caption: **ZeRO memory reduction**: Standard data parallelism (DDP) replicates all model states across every GPU. ZeRO progressively partitions these states: ZeRO-1 shards optimizer states, ZeRO-2 adds gradient sharding, and ZeRO-3 shards the parameters themselves; each dashed outline marks the replicated stack a stage no longer holds. ZeRO-3 achieves linear memory scaling, enabling models with 100B+ parameters to fit on accelerators that could not hold the replicated state.

Behind each ZeRO bar a dashed gray outline at the 112 GB DDP height marks the replicated state that stage no longer holds on the GPU.

figures.title: Matrix partitioning under tensor parallelism
figures.caption: **Matrix partitioning under tensor parallelism**: A Megatron-LM layer pair on two GPUs, read left to right. The first layer (for example, QKV or the first feed-forward layer) is split by columns, $\ColumnParallelWeightMatrix = [\ColumnParallelWeightMatrix_1 \mid \ColumnParallelWeightMatrix_2]$, so each GPU computes its own slice $\LayerOutputMatrix_i$ of the replicated input's output. The second layer is split by rows, $\RowParallelWeightMatrix = [\RowParallelWeightMatrix_1 ; \RowParallelWeightMatrix_2]$, so each slice feeds its matching shard on the same GPU without communication. The only collective is the amber AllReduce that sums the partial outputs $\RowParallelOutputMatrix_1 + \RowParallelOutputMatrix_2$, leaving the full result on both GPUs.
figures.alt: Two GPU lanes, each written as a matrix equation with rectangles drawn to shape. On each lane a replicated input matrix X multiplies weight matrix A, of which the GPU holds only one column half, A1 or A2, the other half dashed. The result is one column slice, Y1 or Y2, which multiplies the matching row half of B, B1 on top for GPU 0 and B2 below for GPU 1, giving a full-size partial sum Z1 or Z2; a note between the lanes reads no communication. Both partial sums enter one amber AllReduce bar spanning the lanes, which outputs the full Z on each GPU.

figures.title: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) AllToAll routing
figures.caption: **Mixture-of-experts (MoE) AllToAll routing**: Expert parallelism on four ranks, one expert per rank, read left to right and drawn for top-1 routing with one token traced. Each rank's gate picks the top-$\RoutedExpertCount$ experts for its tokens; the first All-to-All dispatches every token to the rank that hosts its expert, the experts compute, and a second All-to-All returns the results so each rank can form the gate-weighted sum for its own tokens. In both exchanges every rank may send to every other rank, which is why the pattern stresses the fabric's bisection bandwidth.

A second amber return band carries each token back to its home rank, where the four chips reappear in their original order shaded blue. The route of token a, from rank 0 to Expert 2 and back, is drawn heavier.

figures.title: Parallelism strategy decision framework
figures.caption: **Parallelism strategy decision framework**: A selection guide that begins with memory fit. For a model that fits on one device, evaluate data parallelism against the throughput target and input-delivery budget; the complete dataset need not fit in accelerator memory. A model that does not fit is routed by the structure that breaks the budget, with sequential depth leading to pipeline parallelism, an oversized single layer to tensor parallelism, and otherwise sharded data parallelism (FSDP/ZeRO). Combine parallelism axes when the workload requires them. Peak memory, global batch, bandwidth, and workload imbalance constrain every candidate.
figures.alt: Decision tree flowchart. From the workload profile, diamonds ask whether the model fits on one GPU, whether one GPU meets the target, whether the layer stack is deep, and whether a single layer is too large. Outcomes are single device, data parallel, pipeline parallel, tensor parallel, or sharded data parallel (FSDP, ZeRO), each with a small glyph of layer bars inside GPU frames: one full stack for a single device, three full copies for data parallel, two frames holding upper and lower layer groups for pipeline parallel, two frames each holding one half of every layer for tensor parallel, and three frames each holding a different one-third slice of every layer, the rest dashed, for sharded data parallel. Dashed lines from the four parallel outcomes lead to a box that combines axes as TP times PP times DP.

figures.caption: **Fail-stop vs. Byzantine failures**: In the fail-stop model (left), a failed worker simply ceases to send messages, which a timeout flags as suspect without distinguishing a crash from delay or isolation. figures.caption: **Hierarchy of failure domains**: Failure domains are often nested or overlapping. A GPU failure affects one device. figures.title: Error masking
figures.caption: **Error masking**: Follow a soft error from the top. It becomes a failure only if the corrupted data is read and then also produces incorrect output; at each No branch it is masked, first by microarchitectural effects (unused components, overwritten values, squashed speculative instructions) and then by software effects (dead instructions, logical and compare operations, uninfluential branches). Because software-level fault injection sees only the second filter, it can misestimate a system's true resilience to transient errors.
figures.alt: Flowchart starting at a soft error. A decision diamond asks whether corrupted data is read; No leads to masked in the microarchitecture. Yes leads to a second diamond asking whether output is incorrect or the system crashes; No leads to masked in software, Yes leads to failure. Beside each masked outcome, three masking causes are listed: unused component, overwritten value, and squashed speculation for the microarchitecture; dead instruction, logical or compare op, and uninfluential branch for software. The failure path, Yes and then Yes from soft error to failure, is drawn as a heavy red spine; the No exits are thin gray arrows. A dashed arrow labeled software fault injection enters the spine after the first diamond, and a shaded region below that point, labeled view of software fault injection, encloses only the second diamond, its masked exit, and the failure.

figures.title: Checkpoint-recovery timeline
figures.caption: **Checkpoint-recovery timeline**: A training run alternates productive compute (blue) with durable checkpoint writes (green). When a failure strikes, all compute since the last completed checkpoint is lost (red hatching), and the job must then read the checkpoint and restart (red) before productive compute resumes. A failure therefore costs the rework since the last save plus the recovery latency; the Young-Daly interval trades the first of these against the write time paid at every checkpoint.

figures.title: Distributed checkpoint architecture
figures.caption: **Distributed checkpoint architecture**: Centralized vs. sharded checkpoint writes. In the centralized pattern (left), every worker funnels its shard through one coordinator, whose ingress bandwidth and buffering constrain the write path and whose failure halts the save. In the distributed pattern (right), each worker writes its own shard to local NVMe in parallel and a background process drains the shards to remote object storage, so the local blocking write time can remain roughly constant with fixed shard sizes and sufficient staging bandwidth; shared drain capacity still limits completion.

figures.title: Elastic training recovery

figures.title: The three pillars of observability
figures.caption: **The three pillars of observability**: Diagnosis of fleet failures can combine three signal types. Metrics reveal *when* and *where* a problem occurs (for example, GPU utilization drops). Logs provide the *what* through event context (for example, an out-of-memory exception). Traces expose the *request path* by linking events across the distributed lifecycle (for example, identifying the request that triggered the memory spike). A single signal can justify immediate mitigation; joining signals on shared identifiers strengthens diagnosis without proving the cause.

Logs, labeled what happened: a stream of gray log lines with one red monospace line reading OOM exception. Traces, labeled request path: a waterfall of nested span bars with one long span outlined in red. In each panel a dashed violet connector leaves the red anomaly, the end of the utilization drop, the end of the OOM line, and the end of the red span, and runs down as an arrow into a bar reading correlate on shared identifiers, listing request, trace, model version, feature version, and deployment, which leads to a recovery action box: shed load, restart, roll back, or degrade.

figures.title: Scheduling trade-offs across competing fleet objectives
figures.caption: **Scheduling trade-offs across competing fleet objectives**: A four-way trade-off diamond (Throughput, Latency, Fairness, Cost Efficiency) illustrates the tensions governing cluster scheduling. Throughput favors long, unbroken runs; Latency favors aggressive preemption for interactive jobs; Resource-share fairness can constrain placement to equalize shares; and Cost Efficiency uses discounted, interruptible capacity. Cost efficiency, at left: three spot blocks separated by two red preemption ticks, each tick followed by a red hatched stretch of redone work; gives up preemption overhead. Fairness, at right: team A holds half the pool for the whole period, team B holds the other half briefly and the rest of its share sits idle with a dashed outline; gives up peak utilization. Latency, at bottom: the gang block is cut by two red preemption ticks so short gray jobs can start, leaving the gang in fragments; gives up large gangs, which fragment. figures.title: The distributed deadlock (hold and wait)
figures.caption: **The distributed deadlock (hold and wait)**: In a non-gang scheduler (left), job J1 acquires half the cluster and waits for the rest, while job J2 acquires the other half and waits for J1 to release its GPUs. Neither can proceed, and 100 percent of the cluster sits idle. Gang scheduling (right) solves this by mandating atomic allocation: a job is either granted its entire $\DeviceCount$-GPU requirement simultaneously or it waits in the queue without holding any resources.

Right, gang scheduling: a blue J1 block spans all eight rows, then a blue J2 block spans all eight rows after it, each labeled all 8 at once; above them, J2 waits in the queue in a dashed violet box labeled holds 0 until an arrow labeled J1 finishes drops it into the GPUs. The panel reads no partial holds, no deadlock.

figures.title: Architectural paradigms: Slurm vs. Kubernetes
figures.caption: **Architectural paradigms: Slurm vs. Kubernetes**: Slurm (left) uses an imperative batch model where users submit explicit resource requests to a centralized controller (`slurmctld`) providing deterministic atomic allocation. Right, Kubernetes, drawn as a closed loop: a desired-state file applied with kubectl flows into the API server and etcd, which holds two slots reading desired 4 pods and observed 3. Three violet arrows then form a cycle labeled reconcile loop: watch, from etcd down to the controllers, which act on the gap; recreate, from the controllers to a group of four pods, of which Pod 3 is drawn red and dashed and labeled failed; and status, from the pods back up into etcd. figures.title: Elastic training worker lifecycle and state machine
figures.caption: **Elastic training worker lifecycle and state machine**: The state machine governing dynamic worker membership. Active training loops on step completion and leaves that state along three paths: idle GPUs trigger scale up, a preemption for higher-priority work triggers scale down, and a host timeout or ECC error triggers worker replacement. Each path rebuilds the communication group and returns to active training (dashed arrows), and a spot reclamation deadline can force a shrinking job straight into replacement. Worker processes may restart during resizing, so recovery requires the application to restore valid training state.
figures.alt: State machine with a central active training state that has a step completion self-loop. Solid arrows lead from it to scale up on idle GPUs, to scale down on preemption, and to replace worker on host timeout or ECC error. Dashed arrows return to active training labeled group rebuilt, ranks released, and spare joined. A red dashed arrow labeled spot reclaim deadline runs from scale down to replace worker.

figures.title: Capacity reservation tiers and portfolio optimization
figures.caption: **Capacity reservation tiers and portfolio optimization**: This constructed portfolio combines reserved physical capacity, on-demand acquisitions, and interruptible workers. Reserved capacity covers the steady 60 percent base, on-demand the next 20 percent, and spot the peak; these shares and the demand curve are scenario assumptions. A discount commitment alone does not reserve capacity, and on-demand admission is not instantaneous. Schedulers map steady-state baseline demand to reserved capacity, diurnal spikes to on-demand instances, and restart-tolerant training to discounted spot pools. The area under the curve is filled with the color of the tier that serves it: blue below 60 percent, yellow between 60 and 80, and green above 80. Inside the reserved tier, the area above the curve is hatched and labeled reserved, idle, while the on-demand and spot tiers stay white wherever demand does not reach them.

figures.title: Iron law diagnostic flowchart
figures.caption: **Iron law diagnostic flowchart**: A troubleshooting flow that starts from a missed step-time or token-latency target and low accelerator utilization, branches through I/O, CPU, and communication-overhead checks, and classifies the workload as compute-bound or memory-bound at the leaves. Compute-bound paths point to lower-precision arithmetic and to reductions in active work such as MoE routing, whose saving becomes weight bytes rather than arithmetic in batch-one decode (@sec-performance-engineering-moe); memory-bound paths point to operator fusion, tiling, weight quantization, and speculative decoding. The utilization check's no branch leads down into a panel titled Intensity greater than ridge, which draws a small roofline: a blue rising slope over a blue memory-bound region meets a flat orange ceiling over an orange compute-bound region at a dot marked ridge. Below the blue region, a blue group holds operator fusion and INT4 or speculative decoding; below the orange region, an orange group holds FP8 math and MoE routing. figures.title: Block-wise versus per-tensor quantization
figures.caption: **Block-wise versus per-tensor quantization**: Under per-tensor scaling (left), one outlier weight sets the scale for the whole tensor, so six of the seven small weights round to zero and the seventh rounds to one. Under block-wise quantization (right), each group of weights gets its own scale: the block without the outlier keeps full INT8 resolution, while the small weights that share the outlier's block are still crushed. Smaller blocks confine the damage further at the cost of more scale metadata.
figures.alt: Two side-by-side panels quantize the same eight FP16 weights, one of which is an outlier of 58.7. Left, per-tensor: a single scale of about 0.462 maps six weights to 0, one to 1, and the outlier to 127, with the collapsed cells shaded red. Right, block-wise with blocks of four outlined by dashed boxes: the first block's scale of about 0.00165 maps its weights to 73, -48, 127, and -91, shaded green, while the second block, containing the outlier, maps to 127, 0, 1, and 0.

figures.title: End-to-end inference pipeline
figures.caption: **End-to-end inference pipeline**: One language-model request crosses between CPU and GPU twice. The load balancer routes and admits it and the CPU tokenizes it; prefill then processes the whole prompt in one pass and writes its keys and values to the KV cache, and decode reads and appends that cache one token per step before the CPU detokenizes the stream. The strip orders one request's latency, with illustrative segment widths. Everything up to the end of prefill counts against time to first token, and the routing and CPU segments are serving-tax work that spends latency budget outside GPU compute.
figures.alt: Two regions labeled CPU and GPU. In the CPU region, requests flow down through a load balancer and a tokenizer. Token IDs pass right to a prefill box in the GPU region, which writes to a KV cache box. A decode box reads from and appends to the KV cache, loops on itself, and sends generated token IDs left to a detokenize box that feeds a response stream. Below, a horizontal strip divides one request's latency into route, pre, prefill, decode steps, and post segments, the decode segment ticked into per-token steps, with brackets marking time to first token and TPOT times output tokens.

figures.title: Batching strategies compared
figures.caption: **Batching strategies compared**: Four requests of different lengths arrive one time unit apart under three policies; the timings are illustrative. (a) Without batching, each request receives its own forward pass, so later arrivals queue behind earlier ones and the GPU runs four passes. (b) Static batching holds every request until the batch of four is full, then runs one pass padded to the longest request; early arrivals pay the longest wait. (c) Dynamic batching dispatches whatever has arrived when a short window closes, limiting intentional formation delay in this timeline while sharing each pass between two requests. Waiting for an occupied worker remains a separate source of delay.
figures.alt: Three stacked timelines labeled (a) no batching, (b) static batching, and (c) dynamic batching. Each shows four request rows R1 to R4 with arrival ticks, gray wait segments, blue forward-pass segments, and hatched padding, above a GPU row. The GPU row shows four single-request passes in (a), one four-request pass in (b), and two two-request passes in (c). Dashed violet lines mark when each batch is dispatched.

figures.title: Static vs. continuous batching
figures.caption: **Static vs. continuous batching**: In static batching (a), completed slots cannot be reused until the longest request finishes, although completed responses may already be released. Over the eight iterations shown, 20 of 32 slot-iterations do useful work under static batching and all 32 under continuous batching; the hatched idle slots are the capacity recovered when arrivals and cache capacity permit.

figures.title: KV cache fragmentation and the PagedAttention solution
figures.caption: **KV cache fragmentation and the PagedAttention solution**: The panels replay the eight-slot example from the text. (a) Contiguous reservation holds the maximum length of four slots per sequence, so the slots Seq A and Seq B never fill sit idle (internal fragmentation). (b) After sequences finish, four slots are free but the largest contiguous gap is two, so Seq E, which needs four contiguous slots, cannot be admitted (external fragmentation). (c) PagedAttention maps Seq E's logical pages through a block table onto any free physical blocks, so the same memory now holds it; only the unfilled tail of its final block remains unused.
figures.alt: Three panels built from eight memory slots. Panel a: Seq A uses two of its four reserved slots and Seq B uses three of four; the unused reserved slots are hatched. Panel b: slots 2 and 3 hold Seq C and slots 6 and 7 hold Seq D, leaving two 2-slot gaps; four dashed red cells for Seq E, which needs four contiguous slots, do not fit. Panel c: Seq E's logical pages 0 to 3 pass through a block table mapping them to physical slots 0, 1, 4 and 5 among the C and D slots; page 3's slot is only partly filled. A legend identifies in-use entries, reserved but unused slots, free slots and other sequences.

figures.title: Tensor parallelism for inference
figures.caption: **Tensor parallelism for inference**: Computation is distributed across devices by splitting tensor operations. Attention heads are partitioned across GPUs, requiring an AllReduce operation to synchronize results. Feed-forward networks use a column-row splitting strategy that requires only one AllReduce synchronization per block. This partition can reduce latency when saved compute exceeds communication cost. The illustrated two-collective layer uses a fast local interconnect; its NVLink label is aggregate bidirectional bandwidth, not the per-direction transfer rate.
figures.alt: Two columns labeled GPU 0 and GPU 1, separated by a dashed divider. In the attention stage, each GPU shows eight head tiles: GPU 0 holds the first four as solid tiles and draws the other four dashed, and GPU 1 holds the second four. From the bottom of each GPU's solid head tiles, labeled first or second half of heads, an amber arrow carries a partial output down into an AllReduce over NVLink bar. In the feed-forward stage, each GPU draws the matrix W1 split down the middle into columns, with its own column slice solid and the other dashed, labeled column slice of W1 plus activation. The matrix W2 is split across the middle into rows, with GPU 0 holding the top rows and GPU 1 the bottom rows, labeled row slice of W2 partial sum; on each GPU a blue arrow marked no communication runs from its column slice of W1 to the row slice of W2 it holds, GPU 1's arrow routing around the dashed top rows to enter its bottom rows from the side. Both partial sums feed a second AllReduce bar that leads to the next layer. A key reads held on this GPU for solid tiles and held on the other GPU for dashed tiles.

figures.title: Pipeline parallelism bubbles
figures.caption: **Pipeline parallelism bubbles**: (a) An 80-layer model split into four stages passes one request's activations from stage to stage, so splitting the layers alone does not shorten its sequential computation; it must still traverse all four stages. figures.title: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing
figures.caption: **Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing**: Expert parallelism distributes \"experts\" across different devices. For each token, a gating mechanism selects the top-$\RoutedExpertCount$ experts. An AllToAll communication step dispatches tokens to the devices hosting their selected experts, the selected experts process the tokens in parallel while experts unselected by this token may serve other tokens, and a second AllToAll step gathers the results for the weighted sum. Distributed expert capacity adds all-to-all communication overhead.

The lines on t1's path, to Experts A and B, are drawn heavier than the thin line to Expert C. Amber lines labeled AllToAll gather return the expert outputs to a weighted-sum box that applies the gate weights and produces the output.

figures.title: Embedding sharding strategies
figures.caption: **Embedding sharding strategies**: Row-wise sharding places complete embedding vectors on specific servers based on entity ID, requiring a network gather for lookup. Column-wise sharding splits each vector across all servers, allowing parallel local lookups followed by an AllGather, which is efficient for popular \"hot\" embeddings. Hybrid sharding combines these approaches, using replication or column sharding for hot items and row sharding for the \"cold\" long tail to balance load and memory.

Panel b, column-wise: server 1 and server 2 each hold a tall block of columns spanning all rows 0 to 7, labeled dimensions split, AllGather, slices of each vector. Panel c, hybrid: both servers hold the same shaded hot rows 0 and 1, while server 1 holds cold rows 2 to 4 and server 2 holds cold rows 5 to 7, labeled hot rows replicated, AllToAll, cold tail only.

figures.title: Circuit breaker states
figures.caption: **Circuit breaker states**: The circuit breaker protects the system from cascading failure. Closed: normal operation. Open: error threshold exceeded; all requests fail fast to prevent resource exhaustion. Half-open: after a timeout, a limited number of requests are allowed through to probe the dependency's health. Success resets to closed; failure returns to open.
figures.alt: State diagram with three rectangular state blocks, each dominated by a switch drawn as a thick hinged blade between two ring terminals, on a wire from the caller to a dependency box. The green closed state, normal traffic, shows the blade closed across both terminals, with two requests arriving and a third crossing the blade toward the dependency. It transitions to the red open state, requests fail fast, when an error, timeout, or latency threshold is exceeded; the open state shows the blade raised, an x mark in the gap, and a single arriving request turned straight back by a red arrow toward the caller, with nothing queued and nothing reaching the dependency. After a timeout, open transitions to the gray half-open state, limited probes, whose blade is closed but whose wire carries a probe limit bar: two requests wait behind the bar while a single probe crosses the switch toward the dependency. Half-open returns to closed when the probe succeeds or to open when the probe fails. A key identifies the dot as a request, the bar as the probe limit, and the small box as the dependency.

figures.title: Bulkhead isolation patterns
figures.caption: **Bulkhead isolation patterns**: To prevent cascading failures in multi-tenant systems, bulkheads isolate resources. figures.title: Predictive vs. reactive scaling
figures.caption: **Predictive vs. reactive scaling**: Reactive scaling (gray line) responds to traffic spikes after they occur, leaving a capacity deficit (red region) during cold start in this scenario. Predictive scaling (green line) anticipates traffic and begins provisioning before the spike peaks, shrinking that deficit to a brief, small shortfall at onset in the illustrated forecast. Its early ramp does not eliminate every interval when demand exceeds capacity.
figures.alt: Two time-series panels stacked on a shared time axis and a shared vertical axis of normalized demand or capacity, each showing the same dashed demand curve that rises to a spike and falls back. Panel (a), reactive scaling: a gray capacity line stays flat until near the peak, where a dotted marker labeled scale-up begins sits, then ramps up after demand has already risen; the large region where demand exceeds this capacity is shaded red and labeled capacity deficit. Panel (b), predictive scaling: a green capacity line is marked scale-up begins early in the rise and climbs ahead of demand toward the peak; only a thin red sliver at the onset, labeled brief, small shortfall, shows demand briefly above capacity before the ramp overtakes it.

figures.title: Spot-aware traffic distribution
figures.caption: **Spot-aware traffic distribution**: The gateway classifies requests by SLO and routes 70 percent of traffic, the SLO-critical share, to on-demand replicas that face no spot reclamation, and 30 percent, the best-effort share, to discounted spot replicas that can be preempted. When a spot worker receives an eviction notice, the gateway stops routing to it while it drains, and best-effort requests tolerate occasional retries. figures.title: Global load balancing across inference regions
figures.caption: **Global load balancing across inference regions**: A global load balancer routes each user to an eligible region with suitable latency and ready capacity (@tbl-rtt-by-user-location gives the round-trip times this avoids). Each region (US-East, EU-West, Asia-Pacific) runs independent replicas of the same model, and EU requests can stay in the EU to meet data-residency rules. A shared model registry supplies versioned weights to every region. If a region fails, the load balancer reroutes its users only to destinations that still satisfy placement, readiness, and capacity requirements.

figures.title: Cache hit and cache miss paths at the edge
figures.caption: **Cache hit and cache miss paths at the edge**: A query first reaches the nearest edge point of presence (PoP). After enforcing authorization and reuse eligibility, the edge targets a cache-hit response in under 10 ms without touching a GPU. On a miss, the request passes through the regional gateway to the central GPU cluster, which runs prefill and decode. Generated tokens stream back to the user, and a response eligible for reuse can be stored at the edge for later queries. figures.title: Ranking cascade architecture
figures.caption: **Ranking cascade architecture**: To optimize latency and cost, search and recommendation systems use a cascade of increasingly complex models. Early stages (Retrieval) filter millions of candidates down to thousands using fast, cheap heuristics. Later stages use expensive, high-precision models only on the most promising candidates.
figures.alt: A funnel of four stacked trapezoid bands that narrow from top to bottom and deepen in blue, with band widths proportional to the logarithm of the candidate count. Retrieval, using lexical and ANN embeddings, cuts 1,000,000 candidates to 10,000; first-stage ranking, using two-tower models and GBDTs, cuts 10,000 to 1,000; second-stage scoring, using deep MLPs and DLRM, cuts 1,000 to 100; and final re-ranking, using a cross-attention transformer, cuts 100 to 10. A separate column of horizontal bars, with length proportional to the latency budget, grows downward as the funnel shrinks: at most 10 ms, about 20 ms, about 50 ms, and about 100 ms.

figures.title: Local-only, centralized-cloud, and federated learning
figures.caption: **Local-only, centralized-cloud, and federated learning**: The panels compare three architectures by what crosses the device boundary (dashed line), rather than imply a required evolution. (A) Local-only learning trains on the device and sends nothing. (B) Centralized-cloud learning uploads raw data to a cloud trainer. (C) Federated learning keeps data on the device, downloads the global model $\ModelParameters$, and uploads only model updates $\FiniteChange\ModelParameters$ to a federated averaging (FedAvg) coordinator. Data locality in (C) still requires separate privacy controls for updates and metadata.
figures.alt: Three panels separated by a dashed device boundary line. Each device box holds a small grid of green data records. Panel A, local only: one device with a self-loop arrow labeled train and an empty dashed box labeled no server. Panel B, centralized cloud: three devices send amber arrows carrying green record tiles up to a cloud trainer that holds a pooled grid of all the records. Panel C, federated: three devices keep their records, send amber delta theta arrows up to a FedAvg coordinator holding global theta, and receive gray theta arrows down. Footers read nothing leaves the device, raw data leaves the device, and only model updates leave.

figures.title: The edge inference landscape
figures.caption: **The edge inference landscape**: Published inference latency and energy measurements from MLPerf Tiny and official benchmarks reveal three distinct hardware tiers separated by approximately 100$\times$ in energy per inference; because the tiers run different workloads (keyword spotting and small-image tasks versus ResNet-50), the gap mixes hardware efficiency with workload size. Dedicated neural processors (Syntiant, STM32N6) achieve keyword spotting in under 5 ms at 30--160 microjoules, while edge GPUs (Jetson Orin) deliver sub-millisecond latency at 15 mJ.
figures.alt: Log-log scatter plot of inference latency in milliseconds against energy per inference in microjoules. A light gray band labeled MCU/ASIC tier holds Syntiant Core 2 and STM32N6 NPU points from tens to a few hundred microjoules; a slightly darker gray band labeled edge accelerator tier holds Google Coral Edge TPU at a few thousand microjoules; the darkest gray band, labeled edge GPU tier, holds Jetson AGX Orin running ResNet-50 near 15000 microjoules at under one millisecond. A double-headed arrow at the left spanning the bands is labeled about 100 times energy gap.

figures.title: TinyTL adaptation paths
figures.caption: **TinyTL adaptation paths**: (A) Full fine-tuning updates every weight and retains the state needed for their gradients. (B) TinyTL freezes the backbone weights (gray) and trains only each block's bias vector ($\BiasVector$), small lite residual modules beside the blocks, and the classifier (blue). The backward pass still traverses every frozen block to reach those biases, so the saving comes from what must stay live for it, not from a shorter backward path; the activation and normalization choices determine that state.

figures.title: LoRA architecture
figures.caption: **LoRA architecture**: The input $\LayerInputVector$ passes through the frozen base matrix $\WeightMatrix_0$ and, in parallel, through a trainable low-rank path: down-projection $\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix$ ($\AdapterRank \times \HiddenDimension$) and up-projection $\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix$ ($\HiddenDimension \times \AdapterRank$), which play the roles of $\LowRankRightFactor^T$ and $\LowRankLeftFactor$ in the low-rank update above. Only $\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix$ and $\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix$ carry gradients and optimizer state. For serving, the product $\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix$ can be folded into $\WeightMatrix_0$, removing the separate adapter operations when the merged representation is supported. figures.title: Federated averaging protocol
figures.caption: **Federated averaging protocol**: One FedAvg round in four steps. (1) The coordinator selects a cohort, over-selecting to absorb dropouts, and broadcasts the global model $\ModelParameters^{\FederatedRoundIndex}$. (2) Each client runs $\LocalEpochCount$ local epochs on its private data. (3) Clients that finish before the round deadline upload $\ModelParameters_k^{\FederatedRoundIndex+1}$; a straggler that misses the deadline is dropped. (4) The coordinator forms the example-weighted average of @eq-fedavg-weighted-aggregation, which becomes the next global model.
figures.alt: A round drawn on a time axis. A coordinator lane at the top holds step 1, select cohort and broadcast theta t, and step 4, aggregate as a sum of n k over n round times theta k at t plus 1. A gray broadcast line feeds five client lanes. Each client lane shows a green local data block whose width reflects its example count, then a blue bar of E local epochs and an amber upload block. Circled step numbers 2 and 3 sit above the first client's epoch bar and upload block. Clients 1 to 4 finish before a red dashed round deadline, and their uploads join an amber line into the aggregate step. Client 5's bar runs past the deadline into a red hatched segment marked with a cross and labeled dropped.

figures.title: Measuring the local-work trade-off
figures.caption: **Measuring the local-work trade-off**: The local-work setting $\LocalEpochCount$ acts through two opposing paths. figures.title: Gradient compression techniques
figures.caption: **Gradient compression techniques**: Standard updates transmit full-precision values; quantization maps values to lower-precision buckets, such as FP32 to INT8; and sparsification transmits only the most significant top-$\Glyph{k}$ gradients. Row C, top-k with k equal to 2: values at index 0 and 3 are kept, the two dropped values are dashed and flow down into a residual e box kept on the device, and the bar holds two values plus a hatched index segment.

figures.title: Federated personalization architectures
figures.caption: **Federated personalization architectures**: (A) Full fine-tuning updates every layer; (B) head-only adaptation freezes the feature extractor and trains only the task head; (C) adapter-based learning, such as LoRA, inserts small trainable modules beside a frozen backbone. figures.title: Secure aggregation protocol
figures.caption: **Secure aggregation protocol**: A simplified two-client view of pairwise masking. Clients A and B agree on a shared random mask $\PairwiseMaskSecret$; A uploads $\FirstClientMaskedUpdate = \FiniteChange\FirstClientModelParameters + \PairwiseMaskSecret$ and B uploads $\SecondClientMaskedUpdate = \FiniteChange\SecondClientModelParameters - \PairwiseMaskSecret$, so each upload alone looks random to the server. Summing them cancels the mask and yields exactly $\FiniteChange\FirstClientModelParameters + \FiniteChange\SecondClientModelParameters$. The server learns only the aggregate, which can still leak information unless differential privacy bounds it.
figures.alt: Each update is drawn as a row of six shaded cells. Client A's update delta theta A, a smooth pattern of blue cells, passes through a plus s node to produce y A, an irregular pattern of amber cells labeled looks random; client B's update delta theta B passes through a minus s node to produce y B, also labeled looks random, whose cells are lightest where the mask is darkest and y A's cells are darkest. Between the clients, a row of irregular gray cells is the shared mask s from key agreement, linked by dashed lines to both mask nodes. Amber uplinks cross a dashed boundary from on device to visible to server. Inside the aggregation server, y A and y B are added like a column sum, giving a row of green cells equal to delta theta A plus delta theta B, with the note masks cancel, s minus s equals 0.

figures.title: Tiered adaptation strategy
figures.caption: **Tiered adaptation strategy**: The flowchart routes a deployment by the adaptation the local change needs, then by whether a larger update is needed for the quality target and fits the measured device budget, then by whether updates are valuable across devices. Bias-only updates, adapters or LoRA, and partial or full fine-tuning are candidates for increasingly demanding changes on increasingly capable devices, subject to measured resource and quality budgets. The federated card names one common configuration; whether differential privacy is required depends on the deployment's threat model.
figures.alt: Flowchart starting at deploy on-device learning. Diamond one asks whether heavy adaptation is needed: no leads down to the first of three adaptation cards lined up left to right; yes leads to diamond two, compute and energy sufficient, whose no branch leads to the second card and whose yes branch leads to the third. Each card carries a small branch tag at its top, lightweight, moderate, and full from left to right, and is drawn around a large four-layer stack whose blue trainable share grows from left to right: bias-only BitFit on microcontrollers shows gray layers each holding a small blue chip labeled b; adapters or LoRA on mobile NPUs shows gray layers each with a blue adapter beside it; partial or full fine-tuning on wall-powered edge servers and high-end GPUs shows all four layers blue. All three cards join into diamond three, updates valuable across devices: no leads to a local-only adaptation card, shadow validation and drift monitoring, marked by one device with a self-loop arrow; yes leads to a violet federated card, FedAvg plus differential privacy, fleet model synchronization, marked by three devices sending amber arrows up to a global theta box.

figures.title: Dependency-aware model registry
figures.caption: **Dependency-aware model registry**: A version bump on embedding model $\Glyph{E}$ starts a traversal of the registry's recorded downstream edges: retrieval $\Glyph{R}$, rankers $\Glyph{K}_1$ to $\Glyph{K}_3$, and ensemble $\Glyph{M}$ form the impact set (dashed region) that must be re-evaluated before $\Glyph{E}$ v3.2 ships. A model with no recorded edge from $\Glyph{E}$, such as fraud model $\Glyph{F}$, is not flagged, which is why an unrecorded dependency is a silent risk. figures.title: Feature store architecture
figures.caption: **Feature store architecture**: A dual-store architecture resolves the conflict between training (high-throughput batch scans) and serving (low-latency point lookups). One set of feature definitions drives materialization from batch and streaming sources into an offline store, which keeps full history for point-in-time training joins (the throughput path, top), and an online store, which keeps the latest value per entity for serving lookups (the latency path, bottom). Shared definitions support compatible feature meanings; materialization and historical-availability checks must verify that contract.

The online store is drawn as three key cells, each with one latest-value cell; one value cell is outlined and sends an arrow labeled lookup to a blue serving box labeled point lookups, under the heading latency path.

figures.title: Point-in-time correctness
figures.caption: **Point-in-time correctness**: A training example at noon should see only the clicks already logged by noon (solid green, 4), not the clicks that arrive later (dashed gray). A naive join that reads the midnight batch value of `total_clicks_today` counts all 10 and leaks six future events into the example. A point-in-time join pairs each training event with feature values as they existed *at the event timestamp*, so the example contains only information that would have been available at inference time.

A red dashed bracket spans all ten clicks, labeled 10 clicks by midnight, with an arrow to a red box reading naive join, midnight value, total_clicks_today equals 10.

figures.title: Shadow and canary deployment
figures.caption: **Shadow and canary deployment**: In shadow deployment (A), the proxy mirrors all production traffic to the candidate; users receive only the production response, and both outputs are compared offline. No user sees the candidate's output, but mirroring every request doubles inference load, so the shadow path needs its own capacity and must be isolated so it cannot slow production. In canary deployment (B), the splitter sends a small weighted slice of live traffic to the candidate (here the 5 percent stage) and widens it through the 1, 5, 25, 50, and 100 percent stages as evidence accumulates, rolling back if SLO or error metrics drift.
figures.alt: Two panels. Panel A, shadow deployment: live traffic enters an amber traffic proxy. One lane carries a row of 20 solid request ticks labeled every request to the production model, whose output becomes the user response; a second dashed lane carries 20 hollow ticks labeled every request, copied, to a dashed candidate shadow model, labeled 2 times inference load, whose output is logged but not returned. Both outputs feed a violet offline diff box comparing outputs and latency. Panel B, canary deployment: live traffic enters an amber traffic splitter. The production lane, labeled 95 percent, carries 19 of the 20 request ticks with one empty slot, and the candidate canary lane, labeled 5 percent, carries the single tick from that slot. Beside it, five bars drawn to scale show canary shares of 1, 5, 25, 50, and 100 percent with the 5 percent bar highlighted, above a red dashed box reading roll back if SLO or error metrics drift.

figures.title: Interleaving vs. A/B testing
figures.caption: **Interleaving vs. A/B testing**: (A) A/B testing splits users into cohorts, and each cohort sees only one ranker's list, so the comparison is between cohort means and must overcome the variation between users. (B) Interleaving has both rankers rank the same query for each user and merges the results into one list (here by team draft); each click is credited to the ranker that contributed the item, so every user supplies a paired, within-user comparison. That pairing can make ranker-preference screening more sample-efficient; it does not measure the full deployment outcome assessed by an A/B test [@netflix2017interleaving].
figures.alt: Two panels. Panel A, A/B testing: a row of eight user circles, four blue labeled cohort 1 at 50 percent and four gray labeled cohort 2 at 50 percent. Cohort 1 sees a list of blue items A1 to A3 labeled ranker A only, cohort 2 sees gray items B1 to B3 labeled ranker B only, and each list leads to its own mean box; a bracket joins the two means above the label compare the two cohorts' means. Panel B, interleaving: a box reading each user, one query feeds ranker A's blue list A1 to A3 and ranker B's gray list B1 to B3, which merge into one middle list labeled merged list alternating A1, B1, A2, B2, with a thin connector from each source item to its merged slot. A click dot on the edge of merged A2 routes to a credit A box and a click dot on the edge of merged B2 routes to a credit B box; a bracket joins them above the label credit each click to its source ranker.

figures.title: Organizational patterns for ML
figures.caption: **Organizational patterns for ML**: (A) A centralized platform team gives every model team the same infrastructure, but all requests pass through one shared queue, which can become the bottleneck. (B) Embedded teams each build their own tooling, which is fast locally but duplicates infrastructure and lets stacks diverge. (C) A hybrid keeps a core platform and places ML engineers (MLE) inside model teams as liaisons, balancing standardization with responsiveness.

figures.title: ML system attack surface
figures.caption: **ML system attack surface**: Red arrows mark where an adversary enters the system: the training data, the training job and its dependencies, the stored weights, the serving API, and the infrastructure beneath all three layers. figures.title: Threat prioritization matrix
figures.caption: **Threat prioritization matrix**: Likelihood and impact place each example threat in a quadrant, and the quadrant sets the response. Likely, damaging threats such as federated data poisoning warrant automated defenses; rare but severe threats such as hardware side channels justify preparation in high-value deployments; likely but lower-impact extraction calls for API limits; and membership inference through a public API is monitored and reassessed when the training data is sensitive. Dashed arrows show how deployment assumptions move a threat to another quadrant.

Two dashed arrows move threats to new positions: side channels shift right toward higher likelihood with sensitive co-tenants or exposed edge hardware, and membership inference shifts up toward higher impact with sensitive training data.

figures.title: Model theft strategies

figures.title: Data poisoning as bilevel optimization
figures.caption: **Data poisoning as bilevel optimization**: The attacker (outer loop) chooses poisoning data $\PoisoningDataset$ to raise the trained model's loss on a test set, the untargeted form drawn here, or, for a targeted attack, to lower its loss on the attacker's chosen label. The system (inner loop) attempts to minimize its training loss on the combined dataset $\CleanTrainingDataset \cup \PoisoningDataset$. The nested attack objective can require repeated training evaluations or approximations. It does not imply that every poisoning defense must simulate full training.
figures.alt: A red attacker box at top holds the outer objective, maximizing test loss over the poison set subject to a size budget. A red arrow labeled inject leads to a grid of training tiles in which three red poisoned tiles sit among clean tiles, labeled S union S poison. A blue arrow leads to the inner-loop training box with the arg-min training equation and a chain of SGD steps ending at theta star. A theta-star arrow feeds an evaluation box that computes the target test loss, and a red feedback arrow returns the target loss along the right edge to the attacker.

figures.title: Data Poisoning Impact
figures.caption: **Data Poisoning Impact**: A nominal pipeline (top) and a poisoned pipeline (bottom) pass through the same four stages.
