figures.title: Collaborative Poisoning via Aggregation
figures.caption: **Collaborative Poisoning via Aggregation**: In a collaborative learning setting, multiple clients each train on local data and contribute model updates to a central server that aggregates them into a shared global model. A single malicious participant can inject poisoned updates that the server folds into the aggregated model, so the corruption spreads to every client without any one obvious anomaly. This attack surface differs from adversarial examples because it targets the model during *training* rather than at *inference*.
figures.alt: A violet aggregation server box at the top shows the weighted mean w t plus 1 equals w t plus the sum over k of n k over n times delta w k, and an inset plot of update vectors drawn from the point w t: three amber honest updates point steeply upward in a narrow fan, one red update delta w 2 points nearly sideways, and a thicker violet aggregate arrow sits between them, tilted away from the honest fan. A row of clients sits below: client 1, a red malicious client 2, client 3, an ellipsis, and client N, each holding a row of small green data tiles, with two red tiles in client 2. Each benign client sends an amber update arrow, delta w 1, delta w 3, and delta w N, up to the server, while client 2 sends a red update delta w 2 marked poisoned. Dashed red arrows labeled w t plus 1 run from the server down to each client.

figures.title: Adversarial decision boundary

figures.title: Secure enclave architecture
figures.caption: **Secure enclave architecture**: The Secure Enclave is an isolated region of the system on chip with its own processor, random-number generator, public-key accelerator, AES engine, and root keys. The application processor reaches it only through a mailbox, enclave memory in DRAM passes through a memory protection engine, and storage keys go directly to the inline AES engine, so a compromised application processor never holds them. Source: Apple.
figures.alt: Block diagram. A system-on-chip frame holds an application processor and a Secure Enclave region containing an enclave processor, TRNG, memory protection engine, PKA, AES engine, and root keys. Arrows connect the application processor to DRAM and to the enclave through a mailbox, the memory protection engine to an encrypted enclave region of DRAM, the enclave to secure storage over I2C, and the root keys to a storage AES engine that writes encrypted data to NAND flash.

figures.title: Weight Corruption via Bit Flip
figures.caption: **Weight Corruption via Bit Flip**: (a) One corrupted weight $\CorruptedModelWeight$ drives hidden unit $\HiddenUnitOutput_2$, whose output feeds every downstream logit. (b) For an illustrative trained weight $\ModelWeight = 0.042 \approx 1.34 \times 2^{-5}$, flipping bit 30, the most significant exponent bit of the FP32 word, raises the stored exponent from $2^{-5}$ to $2^{123}$. In general, flipping an exponent bit with place value $2^{\ExponentBitIndex}$ scales the value by $2^{\pm 2^{\ExponentBitIndex}}$; here the factor is $2^{128}$, giving $\CorruptedModelWeight \approx 1.4 \times 10^{37}$. The result is still finite, so NaN and infinity checks never fire, yet it can produce extreme downstream activations, depending on the input, activation function, and downstream weights. A range check $|\ModelWeight| \le \WeightRangeBound$ against the trained weight distribution catches it cheaply.
figures.alt: Left: a small network with four inputs, three hidden units, and two outputs; one input-to-hidden weight is drawn thick and red, and dashed red arrows run from the affected hidden unit to both outputs. Right: two FP32 bit rows showing sign, eight exponent bits, and a collapsed mantissa. The top row encodes w = 0.042 with exponent bits 01111010; an arrow labeled bit 30 flips 0 to 1, value times 2 to the 128 leads to the bottom row, whose first exponent bit is red and set to 1, labeled w prime approximately 1.4 times 10 to the 37.

figures.title: The Robustness Taxonomy
figures.caption: **The Robustness Taxonomy**: Environmental shifts, input-level attacks, and system-level faults decomposed into concrete failure subtypes (dark), each paired with its principal defense (green). Each pillar descends onto a defense wall at the point where it enters the ML pipeline, the data stream, the model's inputs and training data, or the weights and accelerators. Software and pipeline defects originate in the system layer, but they are drawn as the cross-cutting pipeline rail on which all three walls sit because their symptoms can amplify or imitate any of the pillars.

figures.title: Types of Distribution Shift
figures.caption: **Types of Distribution Shift**: (a) Under covariate shift, deployment inputs move to a new region of feature space while the labeling rule, and so the correct boundary, stays fixed. (b) Under label shift, class frequencies change while each class's inputs look the same; the bar heights are illustrative. (c) Under concept drift, the same inputs acquire new labels, so points between the old and new boundaries become errors. Covariate shift changes $\ProbabilityFunction(\ModelInput)$ with $\ProbabilityFunction(\ExampleLabel \mid \ModelInput)$ fixed, label shift changes $\ProbabilityFunction(\ExampleLabel)$ with $\ProbabilityFunction(\ModelInput \mid \ExampleLabel)$ fixed, and concept drift changes $\ProbabilityFunction(\ExampleLabel \mid \ModelInput)$; the distinction determines whether reweighting, recalibration, or model adaptation is appropriate.
figures.alt: Three panels with a shared key for class 0 (filled) and class 1 (open) points and red label-changed points. Panel a, covariate shift: blue training points labeled train, of two classes, sit on either side of a dashed boundary, and an arrow points to amber deployment points labeled deploy, of the same two classes in a new region, still on the correct sides of the unchanged boundary. Panel b, label shift: paired blue train and amber deploy bars for y equals 0 and y equals 1; training bars are equal, and the deployment bar for y equals 1 is much taller than for y equals 0. Panel c, concept drift: the same points with a dashed boundary labeled old and a solid green boundary labeled new crossing it; points between the two boundaries are red to mark changed labels.

figures.title: Gradient-Based Attack Geometry
figures.caption: **Gradient-Based Attack Geometry**: Around a correctly classified input $\ModelInput$, the dashed square marks every perturbation allowed by the $\ell_\infty$ budget $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget$. FGSM moves each coordinate by the full budget in the sign direction of the loss gradient $\nabla_\ModelInput \LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput, \ExampleLabel)$, which lands $\AdversarialExample$ on a corner of that square, the allowed point that maximizes the first-order increase in loss. A step no larger than $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget$ in any coordinate therefore carries the input across the decision boundary. The class labels are illustrative.

A short blue arrow labeled gradient of L points up and to the left from x; a longer red arrow runs from x to the square's upper-left corner, marked x adv equals x plus epsilon times sign of the gradient, which lies across the boundary. A bracket under the square marks its half-width epsilon adv.

figures.title: Autoencoder Ingestion Gate
figures.caption: **Autoencoder Ingestion Gate**: An autoencoder trained on trusted data learns to compress inputs through a narrow latent layer $\EncoderLatentRepresentation$ and reconstruct them. figures.title: Model Scaling Laws
figures.caption: **Model Scaling Laws**: In the ranges studied by @kaplan2020scaling, increasing model size, dataset size, and compute consistently reduced test loss. Each law is normalized to its loss at the smallest studied value, so on these log-log axes its slope is its exponent; the dashed staircase on the compute law marks the compute multiple that buys each successive fixed fractional reduction in loss. The figure reproduces source-paper notation, where $\Glyph{N}$ denotes parameter count and $\Glyph{C_{\text{min}}}$ denotes compute; elsewhere this book uses $\Parameters$ for parameter count and $\Operations$ for operation count. These scaling laws explain why larger models, more data, and increased compute became attractive design choices within that regime.
figures.alt: Log-log plot of test loss relative to its starting value against the resource as a multiple of its smallest studied value. Three straight lines start at 1: dataset size in green with exponent minus 0.095 over a hundredfold range, parameters in blue with exponent minus 0.076 over a millionfold range, and compute in orange with exponent minus 0.050 over ten orders of magnitude, ending lowest. A dashed orange staircase of three tinted steps on the compute line is labeled each 10 percent lower loss costs 8.2 times compute.

figures.title: Energy Roofline Model
figures.caption: **Energy Roofline Model**: Just as performance rooflines limit FLOP/s based on bandwidth, energy rooflines limit FLOP/J. The dashed curve uses the dominant energy term (blue where data movement dominates, orange where arithmetic dominates); the solid curve includes both compute and memory energy using the same coefficients as the worked example. At the crossover both terms contribute equally, so total-energy efficiency is half the dominant-term bound. Static and other system energy require additional terms.

A solid dark curve for compute plus memory energy rises below them and passes through an open dot labeled half the bound at the crossover.

Design decisions fix much of the load the later stages carry; manufacturing adds embodied carbon, water, and chemicals; use adds operational energy at the grid's carbon intensity; decommissioning adds e-waste unless hardware is refurbished or its components recovered.

Manufacture drops a brown box of embodied carbon, water, and chemicals; use drops an orange box of operational energy times grid intensity; decommission drops a box of e-waste unless recovered. A dashed line from design runs under all three burden boxes, labeled load set at design time. A dashed green loop labeled refurbish or recover returns from decommission to manufacture.

figures.title: Jevons Paradox in AI Workloads
figures.caption: **Jevons Paradox in AI Workloads**: A schematic elastic demand curve. figures.title: A Feasible Carbon-Aware Schedule
figures.caption: **A Feasible Carbon-Aware Schedule**: Three constraints share one time axis. The job waits, checkpointed, through the high-carbon hours of the grid signal and runs in the low-carbon window only where cluster headroom exists, finishing with slack before the deadline. The equation below the timeline charges the shift for its checkpoint, idle-wait, and migration carbon, so waiting pays only when the avoided emissions exceed those terms. The curve is schematic, not a measured grid trace.

The job lane shows a dashed waiting arrow, then a green block running under the trough, then a slack block before a red dashed deadline line. The capacity lane shows a hatched busy period followed by available headroom. An equation below sums integrated power times carbon intensity with checkpoint, idle, and migration terms.

figures.title: European Electricity Generation over One Week
figures.caption: **European Electricity Generation over One Week**: Hourly public net generation by source for the European Union in week 47 of 2023 (20 to 26 November), stacked, with the load curve on top. Nuclear forms a nearly flat base, hydro follows the daily demand cycle, and solar adds only small midday bulges this late in the year. Wind swings across days rather than hours, from about 27 GW on Sunday to about 111 GW on Thursday, so the fossil gas and coal that fill the remaining gap move from day to day. Lower-carbon windows for deferrable training therefore come from the forecast for a specific week and region, not from a fixed daily pattern. Source: Energy-Charts (Fraunhofer ISE) public power data, from ENTSO-E and national statistics.
figures.alt: Stacked area chart of hourly European Union electricity generation in gigawatts over seven days, 20 to 26 November 2023, with a black load line on top. From bottom to top the bands are nuclear, flat near 70 GW; hydro, rising and falling each day; biomass and other; wind, thin early in the week, widest on Thursday and Friday, and thin again on Sunday; solar, small midday bumps; fossil gas; and coal, lignite, and oil. The wind band is drawn in saturated navy while the other bands are pale tints, and the bands and load line are labeled directly at the right edge, except solar, which is labeled at its Tuesday midday bulge. Brackets on the wind band mark its thinnest hour, 27 GW on Sunday, and its widest, 111 GW on Thursday. Load peaks between about 310 and 365 GW each weekday.

A single gray trunk rises from the band, labeled assessed with telemetry, and branches into one arrow up to each of the three cards.

figures.title: Conditional Fairness Trade-Offs

figures.title: Production Responsible AI Architecture
figures.caption: **Production Responsible AI Architecture**: The request path performs access controls, minimization, and inference. Bounded evidence collection feeds asynchronous fairness monitoring and explanation services. Delayed outcomes support label-dependent metrics; a governed update path returns approved changes to serving.
figures.alt: Two lanes. The synchronous request path, labeled inside the serving SLO, runs request, access control and minimization, inference, and response. Inference writes one green tile per decision into an evidence log of bounded records. Beneath it a row of delayed-label tiles is filled for older decisions, marked outcome known, and dashed for recent ones, marked pending. In the asynchronous governance lane, the evidence log feeds explanations and parity metrics, the known labels feed error-rate metrics, and all three feed a release gate with a named owner, from which a dashed approved-update arrow returns to inference.

figures.title: Privacy Boundaries in Federated Training
figures.caption: **Privacy Boundaries in Federated Training**: Clients retain raw records and contribute clipped updates through secure aggregation. In this central differential privacy design, a trusted curator receives the aggregate, adds calibrated noise, and accounts for repeated releases before publishing a model. Secure aggregation protects individual updates under its protocol assumptions; differential privacy bounds the released model relative to the specified privacy unit. Neither implies a universal ordering of privacy strength.
figures.alt: Three client cards, each holding a grid of raw-record tiles that stay on the device and a small bar chart of update values clipped at a dashed clip line. Each client sends its update into a secure aggregation region, where the updates appear as uniformly hatched masked bars that merge into a summation node; the region is labeled bounded collusion, dropout. The sum enters a dotted trusted curator region, where an aggregate bar chart gains gray noise segments and a privacy accountant meter shows some budget segments spent per release. Only an arrow to the released model crosses a dashed vertical line marked public.
figures.systems_goal: Show privacy boundaries and release accounting in central-DP federated training

figures.title: Model Update Strategies
figures.caption: **Model Update Strategies**: Three approaches to removing a data point's influence. Full retraining gives exact unlearning at the highest cost; gradient ascent provides an approximate update by maximizing loss on the forget set; and SISA training partitions data into shards so only the affected shard is retrained. The accompanying cost model quantifies the full-retraining and SISA cases.
figures.alt: Three panels, each showing the same grid of training-data tiles. Full retraining: every retained tile is shaded as recomputed and the two forget-set tiles are dashed as removed, feeding train from scratch on retained data; guarantee exact, recompute whole model. Gradient ascent: only the two forget-set tiles are shaded as recomputed, feeding an ascent step theta plus eta times the gradient of the loss; guarantee approximate, recompute forget-set passes. SISA sharding: the grid splits into shards S1, S2, and S3; only S3, which held the removed forget-set tiles, is shaded and retrained while S1 and S2 are kept; guarantee exact, recompute one shard, serving by shard vote. A key below names recomputed, untouched, forget set, and forget set removed.

figures.title: Model Interpretability Spectrum
figures.caption: **Model Interpretability Spectrum**: A heuristic ordering by model family. Small linear models and shallow decision trees can offer transparent reasoning, while neural networks typically require post-hoc explanation techniques; size, feature meaning, and audience can move any model along the spectrum. The label under each family names the handle an explanation typically uses.

Prototype and concept models: an input linked to its matching exemplar, exemplars. Tree ensembles: six small trees, each with one dark root-to-leaf path, TreeSHAP. Deep neural networks: dense layers with shaded input nodes, gradients and SHAP. Foundation models: a deep layer stack with a probe reading one layer, probing. Brackets group the first two as interpretable by design, the third as hybrid, and the last three as needing post-hoc explanation.

figures.title: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) Alignment Pipeline
figures.caption: **Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) Alignment Pipeline**: The top lane carries the policy from a pretrained model through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and proximal policy optimization (PPO) to the aligned policy. The bottom lane turns human judgment into an objective: raters compare sampled SFT outputs, and those comparisons train a reward model whose score drives PPO. The SFT model also serves as the KL reference that limits how far PPO moves the policy, so every human preference reaches the weights only through the learned reward model.
figures.alt: Two lanes. Policy lane: pretrained model, supervised fine-tuning, RL fine-tuning with PPO, and aligned policy, joined by arrows, with a dashed arrow labeled KL reference running over the top from supervised fine-tuning to PPO. Human judgment lane: a stack of human raters feeds a stack of preference pairs, each showing outputs y1 and y2 with y1 preferred, which trains a reward model r of x and y drawn as the one dark filled box. Only two arrows cross between lanes: a dashed arrow labeled sampled outputs from supervised fine-tuning down to the preference pairs, and a heavy arrow labeled reward signal, the only path to weights, from the reward model up to PPO.

figures.title: Reward Hacking Loop
figures.caption: **Reward Hacking Loop**: Maximizing measurable rewards, like clicks, can incentivize unintended model behaviors that undermine the intended goal of user satisfaction. In the illustrated possible feedback loop, the recommender serves content and the resulting clicks enter later training data. If optimizing clicks rewards behavior that undermines long-term user value, retraining can reinforce the mismatch. Establishing this mechanism requires evidence about the deployed policy and the user-value criterion; targeting a proxy does not by itself prove that it has ceased to provide useful information.
figures.alt: A circular loop of four boxes joined by curved arrows: ML recommender, optimizes the proxy, serves served content, clickbait and outrage, which elicits clicks, which are logged as training data, which retrains the recommender. The center of the loop reads loop closes on the proxy. Outside the loop, a proxy metric box, maximize clicks, sends reward down to the recommender, and a true goal box, long-term user value, points to the proxy labeled measured by. A dashed red arrow labeled undermines runs from served content to the true goal.

figures.title: Fairness Monitoring Pipeline
figures.caption: **Fairness Monitoring Pipeline**: End-to-end observability for deployed models. Model predictions feed subgroup metric computation across demographic segments; a threshold check identifies performance or fairness regressions; and alerts initiate investigation and may trigger candidate retraining. Validation and an authorized release decision determine whether an update returns to serving; monitoring alone does not preserve responsible AI properties.
figures.alt: Flow diagram. A predictions card of green record tiles feeds a subgroup gaps card, a small bar chart for groups G1 to G4 against a dashed tolerance line epsilon fair, with delayed matched labels arriving from above. The G3 bar exceeds the line and is red; an arrow labeled exceeds leads to a fairness alert to investigate, then a candidate update to recalibrate or retrain. A green branch from the gaps card reads within, keep serving. The candidate update passes down to validation on subgroup-labeled data, then left to a release gate with an authorized owner, whose dashed approved-update arrow returns to the serving model, which feeds new predictions.

figures.title: Bias Amplification Feedback Loop
figures.caption: **Bias Amplification Feedback Loop**: When ML systems retrain on their own outputs, historical bias in training data propagates through model predictions, downstream outcomes, and reinforced data before feeding back as even more biased retraining data. The edges ('trains on', 'produces', 'creates', 'feeds into') show a possible reinforcing mechanism, not a guarantee that every iteration increases disparity. Green intervention arrows mark where pre-processing (data audit and reweighting), in-processing (fairness constraints), and post-processing (threshold calibration) can break the cycle.
figures.alt: A circular loop of four boxes joined by curved navy arrows labeled trains on, produces, creates, and feeds into: biased training data, biased model predictions, disparate outcomes (the only red box), and reinforced bias in new data; the center reads possible reinforcing loop. Three green intervention boxes each send an arrow to a green bar that cuts one arc: pre-processing, audit and reweight, cuts the feeds into arc; in-processing, fairness constraints, cuts the trains on arc; post-processing, threshold calibration, cuts the produces arc.

figures.title: Layers of Responsibility
figures.caption: **Layers of Responsibility**: Effective human-centered AI implementation requires shared accountability across nested layers. From the core Development Team outward through the Organization, Industry, and Government/Society, each surrounding layer enforces norms the inner layers cannot self-impose. External anchors, including ISO AI management standards, fairness testing, model cards, red-teaming, impact assessments, GDPR, the EU AI Act, and sector-specific law, bind these layers to practice [@isoiec420012023ai; @gdpr2016; @euaiact2024].

The tint deepens from the pale outer layer to the inner layer, and the AI system at the center is a dark filled box. Each layer's anchor is written into a gap in its own top boundary, so the norm forms part of the wall: GDPR, the EU AI Act, and sector-specific law; ISO standards and external audits; impact assessments and ethical review boards; and fairness testing, model cards, and red-teaming.

figures.title: From Model Serving to Closed-Loop Agentic Fleets
figures.caption: **From Model Serving to Closed-Loop Agentic Fleets**: The dashed outline in each panel is the accounting boundary. For model execution (a), the boundary holds only the forward pass, so FLOPs per token and joules per token describe it. For a complete workflow (b), the boundary holds planning, retrieval, tool execution, verification, and every retry after a failed check, with the model called from inside the loop; a copy of the panel (a) boundary encloses one of those calls. The cost is therefore counted per useful task completed: the unit of account shifts from one token to one verified result. Minimizing that cost requires evaluating the whole loop at the required quality and safety.

Small model boxes sit above plan, retrieve, and run tool, and the one above plan has its own small dashed boundary. A red dashed arrow labeled check failed, retry runs beneath the stages from verify back to plan. figures.title: Stopping Precedence
figures.caption: **Stopping Precedence**: Before admitting more work, the runtime tests three conditions in a fixed order. A hard ceiling on tokens, calls, depth, or time stops new admissions, preserving any already acceptable candidate for the acceptance decision. Within the ceilings, a candidate that meets the acceptance criteria ends search and goes to the acceptance decision, which stopping does not itself make. Only then does the marginal rule compare the gain per unit cost with $\MarginalStoppingThreshold$. figures.title: One operation, many attempts
figures.caption: **One operation, many attempts**: The runtime creates the operation ID once and gives each attempt a fresh attempt ID, so a timeout leads either to another attempt of the same intent or, once attempts run out, to an unresolved outcome. The endpoint's lookup, scoped to caller and resource within its retention window, decides whether a request returns a retained result, a pending status, or an ID conflict, or executes. Only the last branch applies the effect. Recording the result inside the same transaction boundary, where the effect permits one, keeps a crash from leaving an applied effect without the record that deduplicates its retries.
figures.alt: Two-part flow diagram. On the left, a runtime column: admit intent creates the op ID once; attempt k, drawn as a stack of cards, keeps the same op ID with a new attempt ID; a red timeout box with effect unknown loops back to the attempt and leads, dashed, to an unresolved box once attempts are exhausted. A request arrow goes to an endpoint lookup of the op ID scoped to caller, resource, and retention window, and a dashed reply returns. The lookup fans out to four outcomes: completed returns the retained result, still running returns a pending status, payload differs is an ID conflict, and not found executes. A bracket marks the first three as no new effect; only not found continues into a dashed box labeled one transaction, which holds apply effect followed by record result.
figures.systems_goal: Show how repeated attempts avoid repeating one logical effect under an endpoint contract.

figures.title: Bounded capture before staging
figures.caption: **Bounded capture before staging**: The adapter drains each bounded pipe from one readiness loop, so neither channel stalls the child, and enforces a byte limit and a deadline on capture. The head fills once, the tail ring overwrites its oldest bytes, and the middle is counted but not kept, so capture memory stays fixed however long the process writes. The staged observation carries status, head, a notice of the measured omission, and tail within the byte budget $\ObservationByteBudget$; a retained record, when authorized, lets later calls read omitted ranges by handle.

The loop emits an output stream of any length, drawn as a bar along a time axis: a head segment, a long hatched middle that is counted but not kept, and a tail segment. Below it, a fixed-size capture memory holds a full linear head buffer, an omission count that keeps no bytes, and a tail ring buffer that overwrites its oldest slots. The buffers feed a staged observation stacked as status, head, a dashed notice of bytes omitted, tail, and handle; below the stack, the equation M obs,max equals M head plus M notice plus M tail, and an arrow leads to the next model call, measured in tokens. A dashed retained record, if authorized, serves range reads to the handle.

figures.title: Attenuation and What It Leaves Behind
figures.caption: **Attenuation and What It Leaves Behind**: Panel A derives two children from the edit grant. The test grant is rejected because it requests execute, which the parent never held, even though its expiry is earlier. The scan grant is valid because every component is narrower. Deriving it does not remove the edit grant, so a worker that retains the parent can still write until the runtime withdraws it. Panel B shows the chained-caveat alternative, in which each holder narrows a token offline by folding a caveat into the next code, and only a verifier holding the issuer's key can check the whole chain.
figures.alt: Two stacked panels. Panel A, deriving a grant, lists three grants in rows with columns for rights, objects, and expiry. Each row shows read, write, and execute slots, filled where the right is held. The parent Gamma_edit, marked still usable, holds read and write over repo/ with expiry T0 plus 300 s. A dashed red branch derives Gamma_test, marked rejected, which holds read and a red execute slot over repo/ with expiry T0 plus 120 s. A solid branch derives Gamma_scan, marked valid, which holds read only over repo/src/pool.py with expiry T0 plus 120 s. Expiry bars start from a shared T0 line, the parent bar longer than the child bars. Panel B, appending a caveat, shows an issuer holding key k, two holders, and a verifier. The token grows from id and sigma 0, to id, c1, and sigma 1, to id, c1, c2, and sigma 2, beside the formulas sigma 0 equals HMAC of k and id, sigma 1 equals HMAC of sigma 0 and c1, and sigma 2 equals HMAC of sigma 1 and c2, with c1 a prefix repo/src/ and c2 rights read. The verifier recomputes k to sigma 0 to sigma 1 to sigma 2 and checks every caveat.

figures.title: Where a System Call Lands
figures.caption: **Where a System Call Lands**: Amber boxes run untrusted code, purple boxes are trusted mediators, and the host kernel closes every column. A shared-kernel container sends every call to the host kernel through a filter. A user-space kernel traps and emulates each call and makes a reduced set of host calls. A microVM's guest kernel handles ordinary calls natively, and only device I/O exits to the monitor. Restricted bytecode has no system-call instruction and reaches the host only through imported functions. The columns differ in which interface untrusted code can reach, not in a ranked probability of escape.
figures.alt: Four columns labeled shared-kernel container, user-space kernel, microVM, and restricted bytecode stand on one host kernel bar that spans all of them. A dashed horizontal line marked trust boundary crosses every column, with amber untrusted boxes above it and purple trusted boxes below it. In the container column, an arrow labeled every call, filtered runs from the workload process through a small filter to the host kernel. In the user-space kernel column, the workload process sends every call, trapped, to a user-space kernel that emulates the call and makes reduced host calls. In the microVM column, guest processes make a native system call to a guest kernel inside a dashed guest region, and a VM exit for device I/O crosses the boundary to the monitor with virtual devices, which makes host calls. In the restricted bytecode column, a module with linear memory reaches a runtime with host imports through imported functions only, and the runtime makes host calls for imports.

figures.title: Two Enforcement Points Outside the Guest
figures.caption: **Two Enforcement Points Outside the Guest**: The packet filter sees only addresses and ports, so it admits connections to the mediator and drops a direct socket or a lookup sent toward an outside resolver, whatever name the program had in mind. The mediator interprets the request. It resolves its own fixed destinations, admits the repository fetch, and adds the brokered credential, while a push or a request for another repository fails the operation grant at the same hostname. A mediator can inspect or change methods, paths, and bodies only if it makes the upstream request itself or terminates TLS; a proxy that merely forwards encrypted traffic cannot.

A fetch of the approved repo passes the filter to the mediator, is marked fetch admitted with a credential added, and an arrow reaches the approved repository. A push or request for another repo passes the filter to the mediator and stops at a red block in the mediator wall marked operation denied. A direct socket stops at a red block in the filter wall marked dropped, and a dashed metadata host box is marked not reached. A name lookup stops at a red block in the filter wall marked no resolver route, and a dashed external DNS server box is marked not reached.

figures.title: A Pooled Instance from Baseline to Reuse
figures.caption: **A Pooled Instance from Baseline to Reuse**: Instances are restored from a trusted baseline into standby, leased to one trajectory, and marked tainted when the lease ends. Reclaiming then follows the reset contract in order: fence the lease's authority, quiesce owned work, export permitted outputs, discard or restore the covered state, and verify that contract. Passing checks return the instance to standby, and a failed check or an incomplete teardown removes it from service. The checks test a defined contract; a clean scan for known residue does not by itself show that every mutable object was covered.
figures.alt: State diagram. A trusted baseline snapshot is restored into standby, standby is leased to one trajectory, and the leased state ends in tainted, marked not ready for reuse. Tainted leads into a reclaiming container with five ordered steps: fence authority, quiesce owned work, export permitted outputs, discard or restore state, and verify reset contract. A red line from every step joins a red path labeled fails that leads to destroyed, marked removed from service. A green arrow labeled contract checks pass runs from the verify step back to standby.
figures.systems_goal: Make sandbox reuse contingent on a complete reset contract.

figures.title: The Prototype Loop vs. the Agent Harness
figures.caption: **The Prototype Loop vs. the Agent Harness**: Panel (a) runs the model's proposed call directly and keeps all state in the message list, so an outside request has nowhere to land, nothing bounds cumulative spend, and calls that policy would gate run at once. figures.title: Trajectory State Machine
figures.caption: **Trajectory State Machine**: Five live states, a finalizing state, and three terminal outcomes. The ordinary cycle runs from READY through CALLING_MODEL and WAITING_TOOL back to READY; a proposal that policy requires reviewed is held in AWAITING_APPROVAL, and pause is entered only from READY. Every exit passes through FINALIZING, which stops admission and resolves or transfers remaining duties before an absorbing terminal state. Each arrow is a guarded edge, and events such as a late result or a usage report can update the record's operation table without changing state.
figures.alt: State diagram. A dashed live-states region holds PAUSED above READY, CALLING_MODEL to the right of READY, WAITING_TOOL below READY, and AWAITING_APPROVAL, drawn dashed, below CALLING_MODEL. Heavy arrows trace the ordinary cycle: call admitted from READY to CALLING_MODEL, tool call admitted to WAITING_TOOL, and wait policy met back to READY. Lighter arrows show pause and resume between READY and PAUSED, no admissible action from CALLING_MODEL to READY, approval required from CALLING_MODEL to AWAITING_APPROVAL, approved and guards pass to WAITING_TOOL, and a dashed path for denied, expired, or stale requests returning a refused observation to READY. A completion request arrow and a dashed arrow from any live state for cancel, kill, budget, or deadline lead to FINALIZING, which branches to three double-bordered absorbing states: COMPLETED, FAILED, and CANCELED.
figures.systems_goal: Teach guarded trajectory transitions and finalization before any terminal outcome.
storyboard: Follow READY to CALLING_MODEL to WAITING_TOOL and back.
Take the approval or pause detour only along its declared guarded edges.
Route cancellation or completion through FINALIZING before an absorbing terminal state.

figures.title: The Trajectory Record as a Projection of the Log
figures.caption: **The Trajectory Record as a Projection of the Log**: The record in runtime memory (top) is lost on a crash; the durable, append-only log (bottom) is not. Bottom region, the durable append-only trajectory log, drawn as a contiguous tape of cells labeled e1 TaskStarted, e2 ContextBuilt, e3 ModelReplied, e4 Authorized and BudgetReserved, and e j ToolIntent test r18, then a vertical line labeled boundary j and a dashed cell for a ToolResult that was not recorded. figures.title: Intent Before Dispatch
figures.caption: **Intent Before Dispatch**: The runtime validates a proposal, admits it with a reservation, and waits for the intent's acknowledgment under the declared failure domain before dispatch carries the request past the durability barrier. Where a crash falls determines the recovery state of @tbl-vol3-durable-recovery-states. Before the worker receives the acknowledgment, dispatch is withheld, but the intent may already be durable if its acknowledgment was lost. An absent intent establishes non-dispatch only when the authoritative prefix is complete. Between the acknowledgment and adequate recorded evidence, including a crash before dispatch, the operation is in doubt; a pending or timeout observation leaves it there. After correlated outcome evidence is recorded, the outcome is established within the endpoint's contract.
figures.alt: A row of five ordered event boxes: e prop, proposal; e auth, admission; e flush, intent ack; a ext, dispatch, in amber; and e obs, evidence. A dashed vertical line labeled durability barrier separates e flush from a ext, with runtime can still withhold on its left and request may have left on its right. Below, a time axis is marked at e flush and e obs, and three bands show the recovery state if the crash falls there: a gray band before e flush, not dispatched, intent may be durable; a red band from e flush to e obs, in doubt, withhold dependent work, which the barrier line crosses; and a green band after e obs, established, per endpoint contract.
figures.systems_goal: Expose what each crash position permits recovery to conclude about a side effect.
storyboard: Advance validation and reservation to acknowledged durable intent while withholding dispatch.

figures.visual: Keep five event boxes, durability barrier, time axis, and three recovery bands with their qualifications.
figures.fidelity_guard: A lost acknowledgment can hide durable intent; after acknowledgment even pre-dispatch crashes are in doubt, and timeout evidence does not settle the outcome. Caption/alt/context review only; artwork not inspected.

figures.title: Live Execution vs. Replay
figures.caption: **Live Execution vs. Replay**: In live execution (top), each turn samples the model, passes its proposal through the authorization gate, dispatches the tool, and appends every step to the log. In replay (bottom), the model client is stubbed and tool dispatch is disconnected, so recorded replies and results stream into the harness and any request the log does not account for stops the replay. Folding those events reconstructs the recorded projection, and running harness logic against them is regression replay. A counterfactual branch differs from both, because after restoring its starting state it obtains new observations from compatible fixtures or isolated execution.

Bottom panel, replay: the model, labeled stubbed, and the tools, labeled disconnected, are dashed gray boxes; the link from the gate to the tools ends in a red bar labeled unlogged request: stop; and the same log cells feed a line that streams up into the replaying harness.

figures.title: Recovery Decision Order
figures.caption: **Recovery Decision Order**: Evidence class comes first, because an unknown outcome admits only a retry of the same operation under its repeat contract (a result-recovery probe or a wait gathers evidence that moves the outcome out of this branch rather than acting on it), while a rejected proposal or an established effect opens new proposals, repair, and compensation. Admissibility then removes candidates that lack authority, allowance with the finalization reserve intact, or time; if none remain, the runtime holds or escalates. Expected cost at a matched endpoint chooses only among the admissible survivors, and applies separately to seconds and dollars.
figures.alt: Top-to-bottom flowchart drawn as three stacked horizontal gates crossed by vertical lanes. A box labeled failure evidence recorded leads to gate 1, evidence class, what is known about the effect. Gate 1 feeds two dashed groups: outcome unknown, which covers one lane, and rejected or established, which covers three lanes. All four lanes pass down through gate 2, admissibility, listing authority, allowance with finalization reserve, and deadline; below it the lanes turn dashed and are labeled survivors only. They continue through gate 3, expected cost at a matched endpoint, repair first when p exceeds C repair over C fallback, per axis in seconds and dollars, and the lanes leaving it are labeled ranked by cost. The lanes end in four boxes: retry same operation under outcome unknown, and new proposal, repair using feedback, and compensate under rejected or established. A red arrow labeled none admissible leaves gate 2 on the right and runs down to a fifth box, hold or escalate.

figures.title: Scoped Breaker Transitions
figures.caption: **Scoped Breaker Transitions**: The breaker trips from `CLOSED` to `OPEN` only when the window holds at least $\BreakerMinimumSampleCount$ classified outcomes and their failure fraction reaches $\BreakerTripThreshold$, as in @eq-vol3-breaker-trip. A late result from an older generation settles its own operation in the operation table and changes no breaker state. Thresholds and cooldowns are policy parameters.

A green arrow from HALF_OPEN to CLOSED is labeled current-generation probe succeeds. A red arrow from HALF_OPEN back to OPEN is labeled probe fails or times out, advance breaker_generation, lengthen cooldown. Below the boundary, a dotted box, late probe result from an older generation, has a dashed arrow to a box labeled operation table, settles, no transition. Beside it, the update T cool becomes the minimum of twice T cool and T cool max sits above five same-color horizontal bars, labeled per failed probe, with a downward arrow marking successive failed probes; the bars double in length and then stop at a dashed line labeled cap.

figures.title: Verdict-Aware Trace Selection
figures.caption: **Verdict-Aware Trace Selection**: Trace bodies pass a fallible minimization boundary into a bounded buffer that holds them until task verdicts, which can arrive late, reach the selector. Selection applies a declared precedence among the classes of @tbl-vol3-tail-sampling-policies, keeps inclusion probabilities with retained traces, and discards unselected bodies. Every admitted trial also enters the accounting record directly, together with recorded drops, evictions, and truncation, so the denominator does not depend on which bodies survived. Assigning high retention priority protects failure traces under moderate load, though severe buffer saturation can still force evictions before verdicts arrive.
figures.alt: Left-to-right flow diagram. An admitted-trials box sends traces through a dashed amber capture boundary, labeled minimize, redact, into a green bounded buffer drawn as a row of eight slots, some shaded red for failures, some dashed for pending verdicts, one gray, the rest plain, held until verdict. One plain slot drops below the buffer, labeled evicted. The buffer feeds a selection precedence ladder that also receives late task verdicts from above. Its four numbered rungs are failed or violation, shaded red; pending or unknown, dashed; accepted, slow or costly, gray; and ordinary accepted, plain, matching the slot styles. The ladder sends selected traces to a violet trace store that keeps inclusion probability and, from its bottom edge, unselected traces to a dashed discarded box. Along the bottom, a violet evaluation accounting record spans the width, receiving an arrow labeled every trial straight from admitted trials and a red dashed arrow from the evicted slot labeled drops, evictions, truncation.
figures.systems_goal: Preserve evaluation denominators even when bounded trace storage loses incident evidence.

figures.title: Staged Release and Its Hold Path
figures.caption: **Staged Release and Its Hold Path**: Each stage applies its own criterion: the lower bound of the paired acceptance interval against the declared margin offline, a divergence measure of tool-call drift in shadow execution, and a sequential likelihood-ratio monitor with hard tripwires in the canary. An unmet or inconclusive offline result, a drift review that finds a problem, or a canary alarm leads to the same hold. The hold stops new candidate admission; outstanding candidate operations keep their identities and owners, and recovery, not rollback, settles their effects.

figures.title: Probes Before Weights
figures.caption: **Probes Before Weights**: Under the default diagnostic route, counterfactual probes evaluate a measured failure in ascending ladder order. A failure that disappears under a probe routes to an immediate systems repair, modifying versioned artifacts that revert cleanly as configuration. Only failures that survive every lower-rung probe reach the weight modification stages, where supervised fine-tuning precedes reinforcement learning. Engineering cost rises and operational reversibility falls from top to bottom.

Red arrows labeled persists link the probes. From each probe an arrow labeled disappears leads right to a repair box under the heading repair below the weights: repair context, retrieval or assembly; repair tool or schema, schema, docs, or adapter; and repair runtime, bounds, sandbox pool, recovery. A red arrow labeled survives every probe crosses a dashed horizontal boundary to a red residual failure box, plausibly behavioral, which leads on evidence to supervised fine-tuning, curated residual corpus, and then down to reinforcement learning, rollouts, protected reward check, under the heading change the weights. A gray wedge on the far left widens from top to bottom, labeled cheap, reversible at the top and costly, global at the bottom.
figures.systems_goal: Route measured failures toward reversible systems repairs before changing model weights.

figures.title: Observation Loss Masking
figures.caption: **Observation Loss Masking**: The mask over a simplified view of the serialized repair example that omits the schema request (selected) and its returned schema (context). Of the segments shown, only the corrected tool call and the final response carry $\PositionLossMask_{t}=1$ and receive a direct loss term. figures.title: Block-Diagonal Attention for Packed Examples
figures.caption: **Block-Diagonal Attention for Packed Examples**: Two independent examples share one buffer. Under an ordinary causal mask (a), every query in the second example scores keys in the first, so the second example can use context it will not have when served. The block-diagonal mask (b) keeps causal scores only inside each example and sets every cross-example entry to $-\infty$ before the softmax, as in @eq-vol3-block-diagonal-attention. The boundary offsets define the blocks; whether a kernel also skips the masked blocks is an implementation property.

In panel b, the same lower triangles are shaded, the whole cross-example block is gray and labeled minus infinity, and the key axis carries the boundary offsets 0, s 1, and s 1 plus s 2. A legend defines the score, minus infinity before softmax, and cross-example score.

figures.title: Exposure Bias and On-Policy Labeling
figures.caption: **Exposure Bias and On-Policy Labeling**: Training only on recorded reference states (a) leaves any state the learner reaches after a deviation without a recorded correction, and the applicable bound, @eq-vol3-quadratic-derivation, grows with $\TurnHorizon^2\ReferenceStateDisagreementRate$. Each labeling round (b) runs the current policy, mixed with the reference at probability $\ReferenceMixingProbability_k$, labels the states it visits, keeps a label only if the sandbox continuation passes the verifier, aggregates, and retrains. A fault-injected record masks the injected error and selects the diagnosis and corrective call. The bound in @eq-vol3-linear-regret-bound applies only when error is measured on learner states and each deviation's disadvantage is bounded by $\DeviationDisadvantage$; aggregation broadens coverage but does not by itself make the training and learner distributions equal.

Beside it, a box labeled reference-state bound gives J of pi minus J of pi star at most the minimum of H and H squared epsilon E. Panel b shows a loop of six boxes: run pi k with reference probability lambda k, visited states, labeler proposes, sandbox verifier, aggregate with D k plus 1 equal to D k union new, and retrain pi k plus 1, with a next round arrow back to the start and a dashed discard arrow below the verifier. A fault-injected record of injected error with mask zero, diagnosis with mask one, and corrective call with mask one feeds the visited states. A box labeled learner-state bound, with the condition disadvantage at most u, gives the minimum of H and u H epsilon pi.

figures.title: Three Ways to Connect a Terminal Outcome to Earlier Turns
figures.caption: **Three Ways to Connect a Terminal Outcome to Earlier Turns**: The same trajectory runs a debugger, makes a faulty edit, and fails the terminal check. (c) Continuation sampling restores each fork condition and averages the returns of its continuations; the difference between the two means estimates how much the debugger turn raised the chance of passing the declared check, with sampling error and without establishing cause.

figures.title: Group Barriers and Version-Checked Admission
figures.caption: **Group Barriers and Version-Checked Admission**: (a) In the hypothetical group of four, the barrier holds every slot until the `{python} Straggler.barrier_str` member finishes, leaving `{python} Straggler.idle_str` of reserved slot time idle. (b) Asynchronous collection releases slots early, so the trainer's version advances while rollouts run. Each record carries the version that sampled it, and its lag $\FiniteChange\text{ver}$ at admission grows with its duration; the long rollout exceeds the illustrative bound and is excluded with its reason recorded. (c) A record leaves verification with a pass, a fail, or an unavailable verdict, waits in a bounded group buffer, and reaches the trainer only if its lag is within the bound. While this admission check enforces a strict bound on version lag, it cannot prevent distribution drift when individual gradient updates make large steps in parameter space.

Panel a is a to-scale timeline of four rollouts lasting 0.2, 2.1, 4.2, and 16.8 seconds, with hatched idle regions after the first three up to a red dashed barrier, and a trainer row that waits until the barrier before an update; a note reads 65 percent of reserved slot time idle. Panel b shows trainer versions ver through ver plus 4 as consecutive columns above three rollout bars, with a dark tick on each bar wherever it crosses a version boundary, so the number of ticks equals the lag. Rollout A, from ver, crosses one boundary and is admitted at lag 1; rollout B, from ver plus 1, crosses two and is admitted at lag 2; rollout C, from ver, crosses four, ends in a red mark, and is excluded at lag 4; in the lag column a red dashed line labeled delta ver max separates the two admitted lags from the excluded one. Panel c is a flow from a rollout pool sampled at ver b, to verification with pass, fail, or unavailable, to a group buffer drawn as six slots with four filled, to a decision diamond testing whether delta ver is at most delta ver max; the yes branch reaches the trainer, which advances ver t to ver t plus 1, and the no branch leads to a box reading excluded, reason and cost recorded. figures.title: Restart Policies in a Supervision Tree
figures.caption: **Restart Policies in a Supervision Tree**: Under the one-for-one policy (a), only the failed worker restarts, as a newly admitted attempt with its own reservation, while its siblings continue. Under the one-for-all policy (b), the supervisor stops the coupled siblings through the cancellation protocol and restarts the whole group from recorded inputs, because the caller's partial work has lost its meaning. Either supervisor that exceeds its declared restart intensity stops restarting and escalates the failure to its parent.

Card a, one_for_one: a supervisor with three worker children; the middle worker is marked failed and is the only node inside a dashed red blast radius, with an arrow labeled restart to a new attempt box with its own reservation, while the other two workers are marked continues. Card b, one_for_all: a supervisor with interface, caller, and test children all inside one dashed red blast radius; caller is marked failed, interface and test are marked stopped, and arrows from all three lead to one box labeled group restarts, new attempts from recorded inputs. A dashed red arrow from supervisor b to the parent is labeled restart intensity exceeded, escalate.
figures.systems_goal: Show restart scope following dependency coupling and renewed admission.
storyboard: Fail the pictured worker under one-for-one and restart only its attempt with a fresh reservation.

figures.title: Majority Review Under an Assumed Error Mixture
figures.caption: **Majority Review Under an Assumed Error Mixture**: Every reviewer has the same false-approval rate, $\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability=0.20$. With independent errors (a), majority false approval at five reviewers (open markers) is `{python} ReviewCorrelation.independent_majority_str` and keeps falling as reviewers are added. Under the beta mixture with $\CorrelationCoefficient=0.40$ it is `{python} ReviewCorrelation.mixture_majority_str` and levels off toward the floor $\Pr(\FalseApprovalPropensity>1/2)$ of `{python} ReviewFloor.floor_str`. At five reviewers (b), the mixture shifts probability toward the extremes, so a candidate is either approved by no one or approved by a majority far more often than independence predicts. The curves follow from an assumed beta mixture, not a measured law of model ensembles.

The five-reviewer points are open markers. Panel b: grouped bars for 0 to 5 reviewers approving an invalid candidate among five, solid gray for independent errors and red hatched for the beta mixture, with the region for 3 or more shaded as majority approves. The mixture's bar at 0 is the tallest, near 57 percent, and its bars at 3, 4, and 5 exceed the independent ones.

figures.title: Three ceilings on the braking base
figures.caption: **Three ceilings on the braking base**: (a) Only the driven wheels brake against the floor, so friction there caps the retarding force at $\CoulombFrictionCoefficient \DrivenWheelLoadFraction \Mass \Gravity$; the credible `{python} BrakingLimits.a_req_str` needs $\CoulombFrictionCoefficient \ge$ `{python} BrakingLimits.mu_min_str` with all the weight on those wheels and `{python} BrakingLimits.mu_min_rated_str` at their rated load share. The inertial load $\Mass \CredibleBrakingDeceleration$ acts at the center of gravity, a height $\GravityCenterHeight$ above the floor, and pitches the body about its leading support unless $\GravityCenterHeight/\LeadingSupportDistance \le$ `{python} BrakingLimits.cg_ratio_max_str`; neither length has been measured. (b) Each direct-drive hub wheel turns its `{python} BrakingLimits.tau_wheel_str` current-limited torque into a floor force $\DriveBrakingTorqueCeiling/\WheelRadius$, `{python} BrakingLimits.force_str` for the pair, and the spinning parts are already counted in $\EffectiveImpactMass$. figures.title: Embodied Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architecture
figures.caption: **Embodied Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architecture**: A representative dataflow. (1) Camera patches receive 2D image-position and camera identifiers alongside language and robot-state tokens; metric depth still requires calibrated evidence. (2) Self-attention mixes the combined token sequence; the colored grid illustrates internal attention weights, not a verified affordance or grasp pose. (3) Autoregressive token decoders emit tokens sequentially, whereas one-pass chunk heads and iterative action experts generate candidate multi-step chunks ($\PolicyActionWindow$) in one pass or over several refinement steps. (4) An independent permission path checks candidate motion against sensed state and modeled limits before actuation. (Synthesized from Brohan et al. [@brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2], Kim et al. figures.title: Measured single-query latency on the application processor
figures.caption: **Measured single-query latency on the application processor**: The 90th-percentile time to answer one query, on a logarithmic axis, for each MLPerf Inference edge reference model on the 64 GB Jetson AGX Orin, the module in the running machine. Dashed lines mark the machine's chunk renewal period and intent revision period; blue bars finish within one chunk period, the orange bar within the intent period, and gray bars within neither. figures.title: The two-processor implementation
figures.caption: **The two-processor implementation**: The application processor runs the learned proposers and has no access to the drive registers. Proposals cross a black-channel board link as framed packets into a double buffer in the microcontroller's own memory. The receive DMA fills a private receive buffer, and the receive interrupt copies each checked frame into the seqlock-guarded mailbox slot, so the processors share no memory. The permission tick reads the latest proposal, checks it against measured state, freshness, and the lease, and sends only an admitted command to the drives, which close their own current and velocity loops. Measured state returns to the application processor as telemetry over the same link.
figures.alt: Three horizontal tiers. Top, application processor: perception feeds an intent model at 2 hertz, which passes a goal to a chunk policy at 20 hertz renewal. Middle band: a dashed black-channel board link, a serial peripheral interface (SPI) bus or a Controller Area Network with Flexible Data-Rate (CAN FD) bus, framed packets with CRC and sequence number, no shared memory. A dashed proposal arrow runs from the chunk policy through the link into a double buffer with seqlock, filled by receive DMA in MCU-local SRAM, inside the safety MCU. The buffer feeds a permission tick at 1 kilohertz that checks freshness, lease, and limits. Bottom: the tick sends an admitted command to drives with current and velocity loops, which move the physical plant; the plant feeds back to encoders and scanner, which feed the permission tick and send telemetry up through the link to perception.

figures.title: Multi-rate cadence and the mailbox exchange
figures.caption: **Multi-rate cadence and the mailbox exchange**: (a) The running machine's clocks during a proposer stall, to scale. The chunk policy renews every `{python} MultirateStall.t_renew_str` and needs `{python} MultirateStall.t_infer_str`; the admitted chunk supplies a setpoint every `{python} MultirateStall.t_step_str`. When the third renewal never completes, the tick keeps executing the admitted chunk only until the `{python} MultirateStall.t_lease_str` lease from the last admission lapses; the tick, bus, and brake onset then put the fallback stop `{python} MultirateStall.renewal_to_onset_str` after that admission. (b) The single-slot seqlock in the microcontroller's own memory, in event order. The receive interrupt makes the counter odd, copies a checked frame, and makes it even; the tick accepts a copy only when it reads the same even value before and after. A tick that preempts a write reads an odd value and keeps its last validated chunk, and a stalled application processor leaves the slot unchanged while the lease runs.
figures.alt: Two panels. Panel a, a timeline from 0 to about 210 milliseconds with five lanes. Chunk policy: inference bars from 0 to 40 and 50 to 90, then a hatched stalled bar from 100 onward. Setpoints: ticks every 25 milliseconds from 40 to 140. Lease: a dashed outline from 40 to 100 and a filled bar from 90 to 150 labeled lease 60 ms from last admission. Permission tick: fine lines every 1 millisecond. Drives: tracking until 150, a short green interval to 172 labeled tick plus bus plus onset 22 ms, then a red fallback stop. Dashed vertical lines mark last admission at 90, lease expiry at 150, and a red brake onset at 172. Panel b, three lanes in event order: receive ISR writer, sequence counter, and permission tick reader, in three cases. Clean exchange: the writer copies a frame while the counter goes 7 then 8, and the reader reads 8 twice and accepts. Tick preempts a write: the counter reads 9 during a paused write, the reader rejects, then after the counter becomes 10 the reader accepts. Application processor stalls: no frame arrives and the reader reads 10 again twice.
figures.systems_goal: Show how seqlock consistency and lease expiry handle different faults.

figures.title: Illustrative out-of-band interlock and STO path
figures.caption: **Illustrative out-of-band interlock and STO path**: Each emergency-stop contact holds its own force-guided relay, and each relay's enable contact holds one of the drive's two STO inputs, so a single welded contact or shorted wire leaves the other channel able to remove torque. The EDM contacts report a relay that failed to release before restart. Removing torque leaves the motor free to coast; the spring-applied brake is a separate circuit that clamps when its supply is removed. The diagram shows a hardware response path, not a certified integrity level or a stopping distance (synthesized from ISO 13849-1 and IEC 61800-5-2).

S1 feeds the coil of force-guided relay K1 and S2 the coil of relay K2; each relay has a normally open enable contact and a normally closed EDM contact. K1 sends STO1 enable and K2 sends STO2 enable to two STO terminals on the drive, which feed the gate-drive supply and then the inverter bridge driving motor M. A red tag above the motor reads tau equals 0, and a note below reads may coast. The two EDM contacts are wired in series with a dashed teal line to a reset monitor, restart only if K1 and K2 released. At the bottom, a brake supply on its own circuit, switched by K1 and K2, contacts not drawn, feeds a spring brake that clamps on power loss and acts on the motor shaft. A note reads hardware only, no processor in this path.

figures.title: Kinematically isomorphic teleoperation loop
figures.caption: **Kinematically isomorphic teleoperation loop**: The operator moves a leader arm whose joints mirror the follower's, and the host copies joint angles across, as in low-cost leader-follower rigs such as GELLO [@wu2023gello]. Because the leader shares the follower's joint structure, the interface needs no inverse kinematics and inherits none of its singularities (configurations where joints align and the arm loses a direction of motion), preserving the operator's direct joint-level coordination. The loop still closes through the operator: human reaction, command transfer, mechanical response, and display delay all enter the recording as phase lag, so the demonstration carries the operator's delay as if it were policy.

A dashed arrow runs from the follower down to a workspace camera, whose arrow labeled t disp runs left to a display, which feeds back up to the operator.

figures.title: Covariate shift and intervention curation
figures.caption: **Covariate shift and intervention curation**: (a) The learned policy's own actions choose the states it sees next. The worst-case cost bound grows as $\CovariateDriftBound$ for behavioral cloning and as $\mathcal{O}(\DeviationDisadvantage\BehaviorCloningHorizon\AggregatedSurrogateLoss)$ for aggregation on a recoverable task; these are bound orders, not measured drift. (b) One takeover. The `{python} DataLookbackWindow.t_lookback_str` lookback reaches back past the divergence point; states between divergence and takeover are eligible for expert relabeling while the learner's commands there are masked. After takeover, the enforcer's blend and the operator's reorientation are retained for diagnosis but excluded from expert imitation targets, and only the reviewed segment from measured stabilization to recovery becomes an expert demonstration. Based on @ross2011reduction and @spencer2021feedback.
figures.alt: Two panels. Left: a closed loop in which a learned policy sends an action to the plant, a disturbance enters the plant, and the plant state returns to the policy, with the bound orders big-O of S squared epsilon for behavioral cloning and big-O of u S epsilon for aggregation written inside the loop. Right: tracking error against time, flat until t div and rising under the learner to a peak at t takeover. A dashed segment marks the enforcer blend, an oscillating segment marks the operator's reorientation, and from t stabilize the expert's curve falls smoothly to zero at t rec. A bracket marks a 5-second lookback window ending at t takeover and reaching back past t div. Below the axis, a row names the four intervals: drift, blend, re-orient, and stabilized. A states row marks drift as relabel-eligible, blend and re-orient as excluded, and stabilized as expert recovery. A commands row marks drift, blend, and re-orient as masked and stabilized as expert labels.
figures.systems_goal: Curate takeover data without confusing divergence, operator reaction and expert recovery.

figures.title: Evaluation evidence regimes
figures.caption: **Evaluation evidence regimes**: The regimes vary along causal feedback (open vs. closed loop) and physical realism (logged or synthetic vs. live hardware). Replay cannot observe compounding drift, simulation leaves the reality gap open, shadow operation locks the trajectory to the baseline controller, and constrained testing truncates failures at the constraint boundary $\partial\ConstrainedTestEnvelope$. No single regime tests deployment beyond that boundary.
figures.alt: Two-axis schematic with physical realism on the vertical axis, from logged or synthetic up to live hardware, and causal feedback on the horizontal axis, from open loop to closed loop. Four panels. Shadow mode, top left, feeds the real plant's observations to a baseline controller that drives the motors and to a candidate policy whose actions are only logged. Constrained testing, top right, closes the loop from the candidate policy through the permission path to the real plant, inside a red dashed constraint boundary beyond which lies open deployment. Recorded replay, bottom left, feeds a demonstration dataset to the policy and scores the action error, with no path from action back to state. Simulation, bottom right, closes the loop through a simulated plant whose dynamics differ from the real one.

figures.title: Rolling shutter distortion geometry
figures.caption: **Rolling shutter distortion geometry**: A phone camera's rolling shutter photographs a turning aircraft propeller. figures.title: Hierarchical 3D dynamic scene graph architecture
figures.caption: **Hierarchical 3D dynamic scene graph architecture**: Five-layer spatio-temporal memory organization bridging continuous 3D-indexed metric state stores to symbolic foundation reasoning. Drawn for the warehouse, Layer 1 captures triangular metric mesh geometry; Layer 2 extracts 3D objects and dynamic agents such as a walking person; Layer 3 models topological places via Voronoi freespace clearance spheres ($\\TopologicalPlaceNode_i$); Layer 4 structures architectural rooms and portals; and Layer 5 establishes global building mission topology. Vertical inter-layer edges coordinate upward abstraction (compressing metric surfaces into symbolic entities) and downward grounding (translating task tokens into metric coordinates) (adapted from Rosinol et al. [@rosinol20203d; @rosinol2021kimera] and Hughes et al. [@hughes2022hydra]).

Thin lines connect each node to its parent in the band above, and the mesh to three of the objects. An upward arrow labeled abstraction and a downward arrow labeled grounding run beside the bands.

figures.title: Spatial belief state machine and transition invariants
figures.caption: **Spatial belief state machine and transition invariants**: Each state carries its invariant inside the box and each edge its guard. Occlusion moves a record from VALID to DEGRADED, where the error bound grows under the declared law, and the bound reaching $\\PositionalTaskTolerance$ or a breach of the validity region moves it to EXPIRED. Every edge back to VALID passes the same evidence guard, so freshness alone cannot restore observability and extrapolation cannot renew validity; leaving UNOBSERVABLE also needs the missing constraint restored.
figures.alt: State diagram with four boxes. VALID, labeled measured, E at most e max, leads by an occlusion arrow to DEGRADED, labeled predicted, E of delta t at most e max, which leads by an arrow labeled E of delta t equals e max or region breach to EXPIRED, labeled supports no motion. Two rails above return from DEGRADED and EXPIRED to VALID under the guard fresh evidence and innovation gate and model revalidated. A bus from all three states, labeled observability lost from any state, leads to UNOBSERVABLE, labeled rank-deficient state, below VALID, and an arrow labeled constraint restored plus same guard returns from UNOBSERVABLE to VALID.

figures.title: Grounded intent pipeline architecture across the silicon boundary
figures.caption: **Grounded intent pipeline architecture across the silicon boundary**: Physical AI system architecture partitioning high-capacity deliberative reasoning on the Application Processor (AP) from deterministic safety enforcement on the real-time Safety Microcontroller Unit (MCU). The AP processes multimodal streams (RGB-D vision, natural language prompts, proprioception) through the intent model, whose computed `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_infer_str` inference sets its `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_intent_str` rate. The 3D cost field box stands for an optional producer family of the VoxPoser kind; the running machine's intent model emits a target pose directly. A producer-side ambiguity filter, which passes only a singleton calibrated prediction set ($|\ConformalPredictionSet| = 1$), rejects ambiguous hypotheses before sending a structured intent proposal over the board-level link into the MCU's own memory; the two processors share no memory. The MCU independently verifies evidence epochs, physical actuator ceilings, and braking stopping reserve before arming the lease timer, whose expiry stops the drives without any message from the application processor; the permission path runs at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_permission_str`, and trajectory admission remains a separate check (synthesized from Huang et al. [-@huang2023voxposer], Ahn et al. [-@ahn2022saycan], and Gray [-@gray1989leases]).
figures.alt: Block diagram split by a dashed vertical boundary. On the application processor side, image, instruction, and state boxes feed an intent model box labeled inference 336 ms, runs at 2 Hz, which feeds a 3D cost field box and then an ambiguity diamond. The no branch leads down to a grounding refusal box; the yes branch crosses the boundary on a board link labeled SPI and DMA with CRC, sequence, and expiry, into a dashed mailbox box in MCU SRAM. On the safety MCU side the mailbox feeds a permission path box labeled 1 kHz tick, which feeds joint drives and arms a lease timer above; a red dashed lease-expiry line runs from the timer to the joint drives.

figures.title: Mug lease against the intent model's timing
figures.caption: **Mug lease against the intent model's timing**: The top lane charges the conveyor mug's modeled target error against the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` grasp tolerance. Without tracking, belt speed exhausts it at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str`; with a tracker that cancels belt velocity, residual slip exhausts it at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_tracked_str`. The bottom lane puts idealized countdowns with zero additional controller reserve on the Safety MCU's clock beside the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_infer_str` inference and the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_period_str` proposal period; each expiry is followed by the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_arm_onset_str` stop onset (hatched). Neither lease can wait for the next proposal. After a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_stall_intent_str` host stall the untracked target sits `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_stalled_untracked_str` off and the tracked one `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_stalled_tracked_str`.

figures.title: Intent lease lifecycle
figures.caption: **Intent lease lifecycle**: A proposal waits in `Pending` until admission either refuses it, granting no authority, or arms the lease. While the lease is held, only a renewal with a higher sequence number, a newer capture, and a passing permission check moves it to `Renewed` or keeps it there; a stale renewal is rejected without resetting the timer. The held lease ends in one of three ways: the terminal predicates complete the goal, the timer reaches $\IntentLeaseExpiry$, or a contact limit or evidence loss aborts it. Expiry and abort both start the validated fallback, which the MCU selects for the measured state.
figures.alt: State diagram. A Pending box on the left has an arrow labeled admitted into a large rounded container labeled lease held, timer armed, and a dashed arrow down labeled refused, no authority, to an end marker. Inside the container, Active has a self-loop labeled stale renewal rejected and an arrow labeled renewal to Renewed, which has a self-loop labeled renewal with higher sequence, newer capture, check. From the container, an arrow labeled terminal predicates met leads right to goal complete, and two red arrows lead down, one labeled timer reaches t intent exp to Expired and one labeled contact limit or evidence lost to Aborted. Red arrows lead from Expired and Aborted to a validated fallback box.

figures.title: Planar laser scanner
figures.caption: **Planar laser scanner**: A rotating mirror sweeps a time-of-flight beam across a horizontal fan, so the device reports range over one plane around the base. A safety-rated scanner of this form adds an early warning field and a protective field. The warning field requests earlier deceleration; the protective field's safety output feeds a controller that selects a risk-assessed stop. Protective-field length must include scanner response, controller and drive delay, braking travel, and uncertainty; a moving base does not become safe merely because motor torque is removed. (Photograph: [Björn Heller](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sick_laserscanner.jpg) / Wikimedia Commons, [CC BY-SA 3.0 DE](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/de/deed.en).)

figures.title: Illustrative emergency-stop circuit
figures.caption: **Illustrative emergency-stop circuit**: Stages 1 and 2 are the out-of-band interlock circuit (Chapter 4); Stage 3 maps to the numbered list above. Two linked contacts each hold a force-guided relay, the relays' enable contacts hold the drive's two Safe Torque Off (STO) inputs, and their EDM contacts in series block a restart after a weld. The spring-applied brake runs on its own supply, and a supply contactor, if fitted, provides galvanic disconnection. A moving motor can coast after STO, so the brake's set time and the physical stopping distance must be measured for the load and state.
figures.alt: Two-channel schematic in three labeled stages. Stage 1, dual-channel E-stop: a red positive-break E-stop mechanically linked to normally closed contacts S1 and S2, each fed from 24 volts. Stage 2, redundant relays with EDM: S1 drives the coil of force-guided relay K1 and S2 the coil of K2; each relay has a normally open enable contact and a normally closed EDM contact, and the EDM contacts in series run with a dashed teal line to a reset monitor, restart only if K1 and K2 released. Stage 3, separate stop functions: K1 and K2 send STO1 and STO2 enable to the drive, whose gate-drive supply feeds an inverter bridge driving motor M, tagged in red tau equals 0 and noted may coast. A dashed box above the drive reads supply contactor, if fitted. A brake supply on its own circuit, switched by K1 and K2, contacts not drawn, feeds a spring brake that clamps on power loss and acts on the motor shaft, with a dashed tag reading brake set time: measure.

figures.title: Fallback responses and the paths that run them
figures.caption: **Fallback responses and the paths that run them**: The plant state and the failed check select one response directly; the four are alternatives, not steps of an escalation. PROJECT, HOLD, and STOP run in the safety MCU's firmware and reach the drives through its arbiter, which here passes the projected command. INHIBIT is the one response that survives loss of the MCU itself, so it bypasses the arbiter on a hardware path that removes gate-drive supply and lets the spring brakes set. On a moving machine that path also removes motor braking, and the machine coasts until the separately qualified brakes take hold.
figures.alt: Four rows, each with a condition card on the left joined by an arrow to a response card. The first three responses, PROJECT, HOLD, and STOP, sit inside a dashed box labeled safety MCU firmware, 1 kHz, and feed a multiplexer whose selected input, PROJECT, connects to an output arrow labeled u act entering a tall box labeled drives and brakes. The fourth response, INHIBIT, sits in a separate dashed box labeled hardware interlock and connects directly to the drives box by an arrow labeled STO, brake supply. The PROJECT condition, proposal u nom admitted, is drawn dashed in bronze.
