figures.title: Closed causal loop
figures.caption: **Closed causal loop**: The Brain proposes across the proposal boundary, and the permission path in the Nervous System admits, modifies, or refuses each proposal before the Body acts. The Body's current becomes force and motion at the Boundary, the World evolves, and the Boundary returns measurements with capture times to the permission path and the Brain. Not every state of the World reaches a sensor. The governance envelope surrounds all five levels and changes on the timescale of releases rather than control cycles. The labels are this machine's values: the intent model proposes at `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.intent_rate_str`, the chunk is renewed every `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.renewal_str`, the application processor sends a setpoint every `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.setpoint_str` over a black-channel link to a discrete safety microcontroller unit (MCU) whose permission path ticks at `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.permission_str`, and the drives close their current loops at `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.current_loop_str` from a `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.bus_str` bus. Another machine sets its own rates.
figures.alt: Five stacked levels inside a dashed governance envelope: Brain, Nervous System, Body, Boundary, and World, with a dashed proposal boundary between the Brain and the Nervous System. Inside the Nervous System an application processor sends setpoints over a black-channel link to a discrete safety MCU that runs the permission path. Arrows run from the Brain to the application processor, labeled proposal, from the safety MCU to the Body, labeled admitted command, and on to the World, labeled current in a winding and force and motion. A return arrow runs from the World to the Boundary, then up a side lane to the safety MCU, labeled fresh state, and to the Brain, labeled observations. Labels give the intent model 2 Hz with 336 ms inference, chunk renewal every 50 ms, a setpoint every 25 ms, a 1 kHz permission tick, a 20 kHz current loop in the drives, and a 47.7 V drive bus; the Boundary is event-timed, the World is continuous, and governance has no control rate.

All inputs are hypothetical design allocations, not measurements.

Panel a is a side-view schematic of a linear track with a drive box at the left end, a carriage carrying a carton, an insertion head pressing down on the carton, and a gate with a red dashed stop line at the right; labels name the drive as thermal dissipation with insulation aging, the carriage as moving mass whose impact deforms carton and frame, and the insertion head as contact force that buckles the carton wall. figures.title: Probabilistic octree volumetric mapping
figures.caption: **Probabilistic octree volumetric mapping**: A corridor traversal reconstructed from raw point cloud into a probabilistic octree and then into explicit free, occupied, and unknown space [@hornung2013octomap]. The third panel is what distinguishes spatial memory from an accumulated point cloud, because raycasting records evidence of emptiness along sightlines, letting the map actively retire a phantom obstacle track instead of waiting for a timeout to expire it. (Image: @hornung2013octomap, Autonomous Intelligent Systems Lab, University of Freiburg.)
figures.alt: Probabilistic 3D Volumetric Mapping and Hierarchical Octree Space Subdivision. Empirical 3D spatial memory representation reconstructed from a physical mobile robot traversing an indoor corridor with a tilting lidar scanner. (a) Raw 3D point cloud acquired during robot motion, subject to sensor noise and finite field-of-view occlusions. (b) Volumetric OctoMap voxel representation modeling 3D space as an 8-ary hierarchical tree, where occupied volumes are probabilistically updated and stored across variable resolutions. (c) Explicit free-space raycasting and lossless octree pruning, differentiating observed free cells (white voxels) from occupied obstacles (dark voxels) and unobserved unknown regions; free evidence alone does not certify traversability for a particular robot. By maintaining explicit free-space evidence along sensor sightlines, spatial memory actively invalidates phantom obstacle tracks without waiting for arbitrary software timeouts. (Image: Hornung et al., Autonomous Intelligent Systems Lab, University of Freiburg.)

figures.title: Diffusion policy architecture
figures.caption: **Diffusion policy architecture**: A continuous trajectory diffusion policy for visuomotor control, denoising a candidate action chunk from Gaussian noise across $\DecoderEvaluationCount$ iterations and dispatching only a prefix of it before re-planning. Asynchronous buffering and an independent high-rate permission path can separate slower chunk generation from actuation. Conditional denoising can represent alternative demonstrated paths without taking their direct-regression mean. (Adapted from @chi2024diffusionpolicy).
figures.alt: Three-column block diagram. Observation: camera images and robot state pass through an encoder to a conditioning history. Denoising: Gaussian noise enters a noise network run for a number of sequential steps, producing a dashed candidate action chunk. Dispatch: a bracket marks the prediction horizon; the first segment is sent and the rest discarded. The sent prefix crosses a dashed proposal boundary into a 1 kHz permission path, which passes an admitted command to the drives.

figures.title: Diffusion policy action chunk denoising and receding-horizon decoupling
figures.caption: **Diffusion policy action chunk denoising and receding-horizon decoupling**: (a) Multimodal resolution: direct regression with mean squared error averages divergent demonstrations into an invalid obstacle collision, whereas conditional diffusion can sample alternative demonstrated modes; generated paths still require clearance checks. (b) Iterative trajectory denoising: starting from Gaussian noise $\ActionChunk^{\DecoderEvaluationCount} \sim \GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector, \IdentityMatrix)$, reverse diffusion progressively resolves a coarse trajectory into a smooth action chunk $\ActionChunk^0$. (c) Dual-rate decoupling: an asynchronous sampler on the application processor sends each chunk over a black-channel link to a discrete $1\\,\text{kHz}$ safety microcontroller, which holds it in its own double buffer and runs the freshness check, spline interpolation, and slew clamping. The two processors share no memory. (Adapted from @chi2024diffusionpolicy).
figures.alt: Three-panel schematic. Panel a: direct regression averages two demonstrated paths around an obstacle into a mean path that runs into it, while conditional diffusion samples from noise toward one of two mode regions. Panel b: three stacked boxes go from a noisy zigzag to a coarse dashed curve to a smooth candidate action chunk. Panel c: an application processor sampler at 15 Hz sends a chunk through a dashed black-channel link with CRC and sequence number to a safety microcontroller with its own memory, holding an active and a filling buffer and running a freshness check, spline, and slew clamp at a 1 kHz tick; it passes an admitted command to the drives.
